From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
President of the Philippines from 1965 to 1986
This article is about the 10th president of the Philippines. For his son, the 17th president, see [Bongbong Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bongbong_Marcos "Bongbong Marcos"). For other uses, see [Ferdinand Marcos (disambiguation)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos_\(disambiguation\) "Ferdinand Marcos \(disambiguation\)").
In this [Filipino name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filipino_name "Filipino name"), the [middle name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_name "Middle name") or maternal [family name](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surname "Surname") is _Edralin_ and the surname or paternal family name is _Marcos_.

**Ferdinand Emmanuel Edralin Marcos Sr.**[[b]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-8) (September 11, 1917 – September 28, 1989) was a Filipino lawyer and politician who served as the tenth [president of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines "President of the Philippines") from 1965 to 1986. From 1972 to 1981, Marcos ruled the Philippines [under martial law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_law_under_Ferdinand_Marcos "Martial law under Ferdinand Marcos"), embracing a policy of "[constitutional authoritarianism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos's_cult_of_personality "Ferdinand Marcos's cult of personality")." Following the lifting of martial law in 1981, a wide-ranging economic crisis, and the [assassination of Ninoy Aquino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Ninoy_Aquino "Assassination of Ninoy Aquino"), Marcos was deposed in 1986 by the [People Power Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_Power_Revolution "People Power Revolution") and was succeeded as president by Aquino's widow, [Corazon Aquino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino "Corazon Aquino"). He was also the father of [Bongbong Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bongbong_Marcos "Bongbong Marcos"), the incumbent president of the Philippines since 2022.
Marcos was born in [Ilocos Norte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilocos_Norte "Ilocos Norte") in 1917. His father, [Mariano Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariano_Marcos "Mariano Marcos"), was a lawyer and politician who was later executed by guerillas for [collaboration with the Japanese Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collaboration_with_the_Empire_of_Japan "Collaboration with the Empire of Japan") during [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"). In 1940, Marcos and his father were convicted of assassinating a political rival, [Julio Nalundasan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julio_Nalundasan "Julio Nalundasan"), but the conviction was overturned on appeal. Marcos joined the [United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army") after the [attack on Pearl Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_on_Pearl_Harbor "Attack on Pearl Harbor") in 1941 and fought the Japanese, who held him as a [prisoner of war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prisoner_of_war "Prisoner of war") in 1942. After the war, he practiced law and was elected to represent Ilocos Norte in the [Philippines House of Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Representatives_of_the_Philippines "House of Representatives of the Philippines") from 1949 to 1959. He was elected to the [Senate of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_of_the_Philippines "Senate of the Philippines") from 1959 to 1965, and served as Senate president from 1963 to 1965. He advanced his political career by exaggerating his military record, fraudulently including claims that he was "the most decorated war hero in the Philippines."[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-9)
[In 1965](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965_Philippine_presidential_election "1965 Philippine presidential election"), Marcos was elected to his first term as president; he was [re-elected in 1969](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_Philippine_presidential_election "1969 Philippine presidential election"). His initial policies included massive infrastructure development and construction, which made him popular but were funded by [foreign lending](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/External_debt "External debt").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-10) During his second term, debt and inflation crises and growing Philippine involvement in the [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War") triggered domestic social unrest.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Balbosas1992-11)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Cororaton1997-12) In 1972, Marcos declared [martial law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_law "Martial law"), ruling the country as a dictator until 1981.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-govPhDeclarationMartialLaw-13)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-fmDeclaresSundayExpress-14)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-lacsamana1990p189-15) His rule was ratified through a [1973 plebiscite administered and overseen by the military](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_Philippine_constitutional_plebiscite "1973 Philippine constitutional plebiscite").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-philippinesReadr-16) During this period, the constitution was revised to empower Marcos, and media outlets and opposition politicians were silenced. The Marcos regime used violence to suppress political opposition, including Muslims and suspected communists, whom he declared a threat to the Philippines.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-17) He referred to his ideology during this period as the "movement for a new society" and founded the political party [Kilusang Bagong Lipunan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilusang_Bagong_Lipunan "Kilusang Bagong Lipunan") to advance his ideas.
After the formal end of martial law in 1981, Marcos was [elected to a third term](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1981_Philippine_presidential_election_and_referendum "1981 Philippine presidential election and referendum"). His popularity suffered in 1983, however, due to [an economic collapse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_history_of_the_Philippines_\(1965%E2%80%931986\)#Economic_nosedive_and_Marcos_ouster_\(1981%E2%80%931986\) "Economic history of the Philippines \(1965–1986\)") and the [assassination of Ninoy Aquino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Ninoy_Aquino "Assassination of Ninoy Aquino"), leader-in-exile of the opposition. Disapproval manifested in the resurgence of the political opposition in the [1984 parliamentary elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1984_Philippine_parliamentary_election "1984 Philippine parliamentary election"). Subsequent investigative reporting on his family's extensive overseas financial holdings[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-18) and false war records led Marcos to call [snap elections in 1986](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_Philippine_presidential_election "1986 Philippine presidential election"). He was challenged by Aquino's widow, [Corazon Aquino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino "Corazon Aquino"). Although official results declared Marcos the victor, allegations of mass [electoral fraud](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_fraud "Electoral fraud"),[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-19) political turmoil, and [human rights abuses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_abuses_of_the_Marcos_dictatorship "Human rights abuses of the Marcos dictatorship") led to the [People Power Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_Power_Revolution "People Power Revolution") of February 1986,[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-20) which ultimately removed him from power after two decades.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-21) On advice from United States president Ronald Reagan, the Marcos family fled to Hawaii, where he died in 1989.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-22)
Marcos, who was viewed as a dictator,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Times_Books-23)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-24)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-marcosRiseAndFallDictator-25) remains a controversial figure in the Philippines, with his tenure widely described a kleptocracy[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-marcosKleptocracy22-26)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-RegimeOfMarcoses22-27)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-28) marked by corruption, extravagance, and brutality.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Times_Books-23)[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-29) His wife, [Imelda Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imelda_Marcos "Imelda Marcos"), became infamous in her own right for the excesses that characterized their "[conjugal dictatorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Conjugal_Dictatorship_of_Ferdinand_and_Imelda_Marcos "The Conjugal Dictatorship of Ferdinand and Imelda Marcos")", coining the term _[Imeldific](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Imeldific#English "wikt:Imeldific")_ ,[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-30) and the family allegedly stole as much as $10 billion from the [Central Bank of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bangko_Sentral_ng_Pilipinas "Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas") during his rule.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-marcosKleptocracy22-26)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-RegimeOfMarcoses22-27)[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-marcosRiseAndFallDictator-25)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-hartfordMcCoy-31)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-32) Despite his removal from office and death in exile, many members of the Marcos government remained in politics, including [Fidel Ramos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_Ramos "Fidel Ramos"), who succeeded Aquino as president in 1992.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-mccoy-33) His children, [Imee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imee_Marcos "Imee Marcos") and [Bongbong Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bongbong_Marcos "Bongbong Marcos"), remain active in Philippine politics, with Bongbong [serving as president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Bongbong_Marcos "Presidency of Bongbong Marcos") since 2022. They have denied accusations of human rights violations by their parents.
## Early life and education
Further information: [Marcos family](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcos_family "Marcos family")
Ferdinand Emmanuel Edralin Marcos was born in [Sarrat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarrat "Sarrat"), [Ilocos Norte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilocos_Norte "Ilocos Norte"), on September 11, 1917. His father, [Mariano Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mariano_Marcos "Mariano Marcos") (1897–1945), was a lawyer who represented Ilocos Norte in the House of Representatives of the Philippines from 1925 to 1931.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-34) His mother, Josefa Edralin Marcos (1893–1988), was a schoolteacher.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Steinberg2000pp115-116-35) Marcos was of [Chinese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sangley "Sangley") [mestizo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filipino_Mestizos "Filipino Mestizos") descendant.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:02-36) He later claimed to be descended from revolutionary hero [Antonio Luna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonio_Luna "Antonio Luna"), a claim since debunked by genealogist Mona Magno-Veluz.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-A.R._Ocampo_2010-37)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-BaguioChronicle2022-38) Marcos also claimed descent from [Limahong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limahong "Limahong") (Chinese: 林阿鳳), a 16th-century pirate who used to raid the coasts of the [South China Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea "South China Sea").[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-39)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-mijares255-40)
### Education
From 1923 to 1929, Marcos attended Sarrat Elementary School, Shamrock Elementary School (in [Laoag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laoag "Laoag")), and Ermita Elementary School (in Manila). He received his secondary education at University of the Philippines High School and attended [University of the Philippines Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Philippines_Manila "University of the Philippines Manila"), studying liberal arts before studying law at [University of the Philippines College of Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Philippines_College_of_Law "University of the Philippines College of Law").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-41) At the College of Law, he joined [Upsilon Sigma Phi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upsilon_Sigma_Phi "Upsilon Sigma Phi"), where he first met many of his future colleagues and critics. He excelled in his studies and in extracurricular activities, joining the university's swimming, boxing, wrestling, and rifle teams. He was a national rifle champion and an accomplished [orator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_speaking "Public speaking"), debater, and writer for the student newspaper.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-42)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_][[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-43)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_] Marcos served as a battalion commander in the [Reserve Officers' Training Corps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reserve_Officers'_Training_Corps "Reserve Officers' Training Corps") (ROTC) and was commissioned as a third lieutenant in the Philippine Constabulary Reserve.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-marcosOvercameMurder-44)
In 1939, Marcos took the [bar exam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Bar_Examinations "Philippine Bar Examinations"); he was a top scorer with a score of 92.35 percent and graduated _[cum laude](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cum_laude "Cum laude")_.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-veraFilesMarcosBarExams-45)[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-46)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-47) He was elected to the [Pi Gamma Mu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pi_Gamma_Mu "Pi Gamma Mu") and the [Phi Kappa Phi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phi_Kappa_Phi "Phi Kappa Phi") international [honor societies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honour_society "Honour society").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-48) Marcos received an honorary Doctor of Laws (LL.D.) (_[honoris causa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honorary_degree "Honorary degree")_) degree in 1967 from [Central Philippine University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Philippine_University "Central Philippine University").[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Honorary_Degree_Recipients_from_1905-1980s_-_Central_Philippine_University-49)
### Assassination of Julio Nalundasan
Main article: [Julio Nalundasan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julio_Nalundasan "Julio Nalundasan")
In 1934, Mariano Marcos lost his campaign for re-election to the House of Representatives to [Julio Nalundasan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julio_Nalundasan "Julio Nalundasan"). Mariano Marcos challenged Nalundasan again in the 1935 election but was defeated. On the day after the election, September 21, 1935, Nalundasan was killed by a single rifle shot at his home in [Batac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batac "Batac").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-conjugalAteneo-50) In December 1938, two witnesses accused Ferdinand Marcos, Mariano, and Ferdinand's uncles Pio Marcos and Quirino Lizardo of conspiring to assassinate Nalundasan.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-mijares237-51)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-52) At the time, Ferdinand was still studying law and a national champion as a member of the university rifle team.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-marcosOvercameMurder-44) On the night of the assassination, Ferdinand's rifle was in its rack in the ROTC armory. However, the rifle of team captain [Teodoro Kalaw](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teodoro_Kalaw#Personal_life "Teodoro Kalaw") was missing, and Ferdinand had access to the armory. A [National Bureau of Investigation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Bureau_of_Investigation_\(Philippines\) "National Bureau of Investigation \(Philippines\)") concluded that Kalaw's rifle was the murder weapon.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-conjugalAteneo-50) Ferdinand and his uncle Quirino were convicted of murder, and Ferdinand was sentenced to 10 to 17 years in prison.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-53)
He appealed his conviction to the [Supreme Court of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_Philippines "Supreme Court of the Philippines").[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-54) The Supreme Court overturned the lower court's decision on October 22, 1940, acquitting both men of all charges except [contempt of court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contempt_of_court "Contempt of court").[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-55)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-puppetPresident-56) Justice [Jose P. Laurel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_P._Laurel "Jose P. Laurel"), who wrote the majority decision, persuaded his colleagues to acquit Marcos. Laurel himself had been convicted of frustrated murder as a young man after he almost killed a rival during a youthful brawl but was acquitted after his own appeal to the Supreme Court.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-conjugalAteneo-50)
## Military service and early political career
### World War II
Main article: [Military career of Ferdinand Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_career_of_Ferdinand_Marcos "Military career of Ferdinand Marcos")
Marcos's military service record, and his alleged exaggeration of it, have been the source of controversy and confusion.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Philstar_-_Imagined_Heroism-57)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-SubSelfie_-_Truth_or_Dare-58) Near the end of his presidency, researchers found that most stories about Marcos's military service were inaccurate or untrue.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-59)
Following the [attack on Pearl Harbor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Attack_on_Pearl_Harbor "Attack on Pearl Harbor") and [Japanese invasion of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines_campaign_\(1941%E2%80%931942\) "Philippines campaign \(1941–1942\)") in December 1941, Marcos was called into service in the [United States Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army "United States Army"). He fought with the United States until April 1942, when he was taken prisoner by the Japanese at the [Battle of Bataan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Bataan "Battle of Bataan"). Official Army records show that he was assigned to the intelligence service in the [21st Infantry Division](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/21st_Division_\(Philippines\) "21st Division \(Philippines\)") under [Mateo M. Capinpin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mateo_M._Capinpin "Mateo M. Capinpin").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Philstar_-_Imagined_Heroism-57)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-SubSelfie_-_Truth_or_Dare-58)[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-TheWashPost-60) Despite his later claims of heroism at the battle, there are no contemporaneous records of any awards or decorations received by Marcos, and his commander and other officers did not corroborate his claims. However, official dispatches reference Marcos bringing a wounded officer to the rear and note that the 21st Infantry Division did not receive sufficient recognition for their actions at Bataan.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-WP_-_Dec_18,_1983-61)
After surrendering, Marcos survived the [Bataan Death March](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bataan_Death_March "Bataan Death March").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMijares1976246%E2%80%93254-62) According to Marcos's own account, he was released by the Japanese on August 4, 1942. This claim later became controversial when it was cited as evidence that Marcos's father had served as a [Japanese collaborator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Collaboration_with_the_Empire_of_Japan "Collaboration with the Empire of Japan"), as the Japanese only released prisoners who had severe health problems or whose families had cooperated with Japanese authorities.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-JohnSharkey198601243-63)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-TheWashPost2-64)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMijares1976246%E2%80%93254-62) In 1945, his father was executed by Filipino guerillas by [drawing and quartering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanged,_drawn_and_quartered "Hanged, drawn and quartered") using [carabaos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carabao "Carabao"). His remains were left hanging on a tree.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-JohnSharkey19860124-65)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-66)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-LaphamsRaiders-67) At least one contemporary Japanese official recorded Ferdinand himself as a Japanese propagandist.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-WP_24_Jan_1986-68)
After his release, Marcos claimed to have led a guerrilla force of nine thousand in northern Luzon; these claims have been contradicted and ruled criminal by the United States Army investigators.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-whScottPrehispanic-69)[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-McCoy1999-70) According to [Primitivo Mijares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primitivo_Mijares "Primitivo Mijares"), Marcos also filed a fraudulent war reparations claim for millions of dollars in cattle.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-71) Military records show that Marcos rejoined U.S. forces in December 1944 until his discharge with the [rank of major](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Major_\(rank\) "Major \(rank\)") in May 1945.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-JohnSharkey198601243-63)[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Curtis1948-72)
### Political rise (1949–1965)
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7c/Senator_Ferdinand_E._Marcos.jpg/250px-Senator_Ferdinand_E._Marcos.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Senator_Ferdinand_E._Marcos.jpg)Marcos in 1960
After World War II, the Philippines gained political independence from the United States on July 4, 1946.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Wood1986-73)[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Dubsky1993-74) Marcos was appointed as one of eleven special prosecutors, tasked to prosecute those accused of collaboration with the Japanese.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-75) Leveraging this appointment and his exaggerated war record, Marcos eventually entered politics as a member of the new [Liberal Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liberal_Party_\(Philippines\) "Liberal Party \(Philippines\)"). In 1949, Marcos ran for his father's former seat in [Ilocos Norte's 2nd congressional district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilocos_Norte's_2nd_congressional_district "Ilocos Norte's 2nd congressional district"). He won and was re-elected to the House of Representatives twice, serving until 1959.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Ferdinand_Edralin_Marcos-76)
The Liberal Party had split from the [Nacionalista Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nacionalista_Party "Nacionalista Party") in 1946. Marcos later became the party's economic spokesman and chaired the House Committee on Commerce and Industry. He also served on the committees on Defense, Ways and Means; Industry; Banks Currency; War Veterans; Civil Service; and Corporations and Economic Planning. He was also a member of the Special Committee on Import and Price Controls, the Special Committee on Reparations, and the House Electoral Tribunal.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Ferdinand_Edralin_Marcos-76)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]
After serving three terms in the House, Marcos was elected to the Senate [in 1959](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1959_Philippine_Senate_election "1959 Philippine Senate election"). He became minority floor leader in the Senate in 1960 and served as party president from 1961 to 1964. From 1963 to 1965, he was [Senate President](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senate_President_of_the_Philippines "Senate President of the Philippines"). He introduced significant bills, many of which were enacted.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Ferdinand_Edralin_Marcos-76)[_[clarification needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] During his 1962 campaign, Marcos claimed to be the most decorated Filipino veteran of World War II, having garnered almost every medal and decoration awarded by the American or Philippine government, including the Distinguished Service Cross and Medal of Honor.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-mijares246-77)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-chicagoTribune1-78) The Liberal Party later confirmed that many of the medals were awarded to Marcos in 1962 to aid in his Senate election campaign.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMijares1976-79)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_][[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-80)

### First term (1965–1969)
Main article: [First term of the presidency of Ferdinand Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_term_of_the_presidency_of_Ferdinand_Marcos "First term of the presidency of Ferdinand Marcos")
Further information: [List of cabinets of the Philippines § Ferdinand Marcos (1965–1986)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_cabinets_of_the_Philippines#Ferdinand_Marcos_\(1965%E2%80%931986\) "List of cabinets of the Philippines")
#### 1965 presidential campaign
Main article: [1965 Philippine presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1965_Philippine_presidential_election "1965 Philippine presidential election")
In 1965, Marcos expected incumbent president [Diosdado Macapagal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diosdado_Macapagal "Diosdado Macapagal") to step aside and support his campaign for president. Marcos had managed Macapagal's 1961 campaign in exchange for Macapagal's support in 1965. Stung by Macapagal's broken promise, Marcos left the Liberal Party to join the [Nacionalista Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nacionalista_Party "Nacionalista Party") and run for president on a populist platform.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:11-81) With the support of Faustino del Mundo, leader of the [Hukbalahap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hukbalahap "Hukbalahap") guerrilla remnants and organized crime in [Pampanga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pampanga "Pampanga") and southern [Tarlac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarlac "Tarlac"), Marcos was able to mobilize resources and utilize coercive violence to win [Central Luzon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Luzon "Central Luzon"), which was crucial to the election.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:11-81) On October 13, 1965, at least one person was killed and five wounded in a clash between gangs supporting Macapagal and Marcos.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:11-81)
Marcos won the election and was [inaugurated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_inauguration_of_Ferdinand_Marcos "First inauguration of Ferdinand Marcos") as the [10th](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_presidents_of_the_Philippines "List of presidents of the Philippines") [president of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_the_Philippines "President of the Philippines") on December 30, 1965.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Kasaysayan9ch10-82)
#### Domestic infrastructure and education policies
Main article: [Edifice complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edifice_complex "Edifice complex")
As president, Marcos launched an aggressive program of infrastructure development funded by foreign loans. From 1966 to 1970, Marcos increased infrastructure spending in the Philippines by 70 percent, and as of 2011, Marcos had spent more annually on infrastructure than any other president of the Philippines.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Kasaysayan9ch10-82): 128  [[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-83) Major projects included the construction of the [Cultural Center of the Philippines complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Center_of_the_Philippines_complex "Cultural Center of the Philippines complex"). Critics have referred to the Marcos policy of major construction and infrastructure building to curry public support as an "[edifice complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edifice_complex "Edifice complex")."[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-84)
Projects completed during Marcos's rule from 1965 to 1986 included major healthcare infrastructure, including the leading centers for heart, lung, and kidney care in the Philippines, and transportation infrastructure, including the [Marcos Bridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Juanico_Bridge "San Juanico Bridge") between [Leyte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leyte "Leyte") and [Samar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samar "Samar"), the [Pan-Philippine Highway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pan-Philippine_Highway "Pan-Philippine Highway"), and the [Manila Light Rail Transit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila_Light_Rail_Transit_System "Manila Light Rail Transit System").[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-85)[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:6-86) These projects were typically constructed on a rush basis, often compromising their structural safety.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Kasaysayan9ch12-87): 169 [[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:4-88) Marcos also emphasized educational infrastructure, including public school buildings and roads to connect communities to them, during his first presidential term.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Kasaysayan9ch10-82): 128  Ultimately, forty-seven colleges and universities were established during Marcos's term in office from 1965 to 1986.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-89)
Spending during his first term outpaced tax revenues, but Marcos continued to promise "rice, roads, and school buildings" as the cornerstone of his 1969 re-election campaign. Marcos covered the gap with foreign lending, leading to a 72 percent increase in the budget deficit over Macapagal's term in office. Although he remained popular for most of his first term,[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Balbosas1992-11)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Cororaton1997-12)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Kasaysayan9ch10-82) these policies created long-term economic instability and required that Marcos rely on foreign support to preserve his rule.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Kasaysayan9ch10-82)[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-theMarcosDebt-90)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-theEdificeComplex-91)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-gma7edifice-92)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Romero2008-93): 89 
Marcos also used construction projects to advance the political and public profile of his wife, [Imelda Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imelda_Marcos "Imelda Marcos").[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Kasaysayan9ch12-87): 169  In 1966, he announced the [Cultural Center of the Philippines Complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Center_of_the_Philippines_Complex "Cultural Center of the Philippines Complex") by executive order, with Imelda serving as its chair.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-94)[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:3-95) Other cultural and heritage cites constructed by Marcos included the [Nayong Pilipino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nayong_Pilipino_Cultural_Park_and_Creative_Hub "Nayong Pilipino Cultural Park and Creative Hub"), [the Philippine International Convention Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_International_Convention_Center "Philippine International Convention Center"), and the [Manila Film Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila_Film_Center "Manila Film Center"). By 1977–1980, projects in the "conspicuous capital outlays" category had ballooned to account for 20 percent of the Philippines' capital outlays.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Romero2008-93): "88–89" 
#### Vietnam War, foreign policy, and militarism
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/51/The_Marcoses_and_the_Johnsons_dancing.jpg/330px-The_Marcoses_and_the_Johnsons_dancing.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:The_Marcoses_and_the_Johnsons_dancing.jpg)Marcos (pictured here with [Lady Bird Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lady_Bird_Johnson "Lady Bird Johnson"), his wife Imelda, and [Lyndon B. Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyndon_B._Johnson "Lyndon B. Johnson")) maintained strong relations with the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") during the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War").
As president, Marcos pursued a close relationship with the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States"), protecting and maintaining U.S. military bases in the Philippines as part of the ongoing [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") conflict. Marcos relied on the relationship to sustain his regime.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:10-96) Marcos also leveraged U.S. interests to advance his political career; for example, Marcos threatened to search every visiting American naval vessel during his 1969 presidential campaign. However, Marcos secretly assured the United States that he had no desire for American withdrawal; in response, the United States injected millions into the Philippine government's banking system, boosting his popularity and re-election campaign.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-97) Marcos repeatedly took public stands critical of United States influence, leveraging the implied threat to secure increased aid.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:12-98)
Under pressure from the [Lyndon B. Johnson administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Lyndon_B._Johnson "Presidency of Lyndon B. Johnson") in the 1960s, Marcos reversed his prior position by permitting Philippine involvement in the [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War") in the form of the [Philippine Civic Action Group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Civic_Action_Group "Philippine Civic Action Group") (PHILCAG), a [combat engineer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combat_engineer "Combat engineer") unit, despite some opposition within the [Philippine Congress](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congress_of_the_Philippines "Congress of the Philippines").[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-McMahon1999-99)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-showingflag-100)[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-agoncillo508-101) PHILCAG were involved from the middle of 1966, growing to a strength of 1,600 troops by 1968. Between 1966 and 1970, over 10,000 Filipino soldiers served in Vietnam, mainly involved in civilian infrastructure projects.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Celoza1997-102): [102–103](https://books.google.com/books?id=Sp3U1oCNKlgC) [[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-103) Marcos secretly assured the US he had no desire for an American withdrawal. He had received warnings from the Philippine embassy that US aid was at risk in Congress. Marcos returned to the implied threats. In one speech, he stated that the bases were a threat to regional peace and security while reminding the US of its "solemn obligation" to continue aid.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:12-98) In late 1976, the US offered $1 billion of mixed grants and loans to the Philippines, but Marcos rejected the offer.[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-104)
Despite his alignment with the United States, Marcos also pursued informal alignment with the Soviet Union within the [Sino-Soviet split](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Soviet_split "Sino-Soviet split"). The [Partido Komunista ng Pilipinas-1930](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partido_Komunista_ng_Pilipinas-1930 "Partido Komunista ng Pilipinas-1930") (PKP-1930), which had supported his 1965 election and was Soviet-aligned, was challenged by the [Communist Party of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_the_Philippines "Communist Party of the Philippines"), which was Maoist, in 1968. Although PKP-1930 was officially illegal, Marcos appointed some members to positions within his government as salaried researchers, and they were then used as an informal channel of negotiation with the Soviet Union and the [Eastern Bloc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Bloc "Eastern Bloc").[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:16-105)[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:17-106)
Despite his general anticommunism and opposition to the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") under [Mao Zedong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao_Zedong "Mao Zedong"), Marcos softened his tone in 1969, publicly asserting the need for the Philippines to establish a diplomatic relationship with the People's Republic of China.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-107) In his January 1969 State of the Nation Address, he said,[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-108)
> We, in Asia must strive toward a modus vivendi with Red China. I reiterate this need, which is becoming more urgent each day. Before long, Communist China will have increased its striking power a thousand fold with a sophisticated delivery system for its nuclear weapons. We must prepare for that day. We must prepare to coexist peaceably with Communist China.[_[undue weight?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Neutral_point_of_view#Due_and_undue_weight "Wikipedia:Neutral point of view") – [discuss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk:Ferdinand_Marcos#undue "Talk:Ferdinand Marcos")_]
During his first term, Marcos developed close relationships with Philippine military officers and significantly expanded the armed forces by allowing loyal generals to remain in their positions past their age of retirement. Loyal officers who did retire were granted positions in his government. He also significantly expanded the military budget, utilizing military personnel for civic projects such as school construction. In an unprecedented move, Marcos chose to concurrently serve as his own [defense secretary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_National_Defense_\(Philippines\) "Department of National Defense \(Philippines\)"), giving him direct control over the military. In 1968, Senator [Ninoy Aquino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninoy_Aquino "Ninoy Aquino") accused Marcos of trying to establish a "[garrison state](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Garrison_State "The Garrison State")."[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Kasaysayan9ch10-82)[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-GovPh29thNinoyAnniv-109)
#### Jabidah massacre and Moro conflict
Main articles: [Jabidah massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jabidah_massacre "Jabidah massacre") and [Moro conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moro_conflict "Moro conflict")
In March 1968, Jibin Arula testified that he had been the lone survivor of a group of [Moro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moro_people "Moro people") army recruits that had been executed _en masse_ on [Corregidor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corregidor "Corregidor") by the [Armed Forces of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armed_Forces_of_the_Philippines "Armed Forces of the Philippines") on March 18, 1968, which came to be known as the [Jabidah massacre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jabidah_massacre "Jabidah massacre").[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Rappler-110)[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-George1980-111) Arula's allegations were the subject of a critical exposé by Ninoy Aquino and became a major catalyst of the [Moro insurgency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moro_insurgency_in_the_Philippines "Moro insurgency in the Philippines").[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-George1980-111)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-sfof-112)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-113) When none of the officers implicated in the massacre were convicted, many [Filipino Muslims](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam_in_the_Philippines "Islam in the Philippines"), especially intellectuals and educated youth, were enraged. They came to believe that the Manila government had little regard for their safety or interests, and efforts at integration and accommodation were abandoned.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-George1980-111)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Larousse2001-114)[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Majul1985-115)[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-MuslimPresident1994-116)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_][[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Smith2015-117) Dissent led to the formation of the [Muslim Independence Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muslim_Independence_Movement "Muslim Independence Movement") in 1968, which later consolidated with the Bangsamoro Liberation Organization to form the [Moro National Liberation Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moro_National_Liberation_Front "Moro National Liberation Front") in October 1972.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-BetweenIntegrationandSecession-118)
### Second term (1969–1972)
Main article: [Second term of the presidency of Ferdinand Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_term_of_the_presidency_of_Ferdinand_Marcos "Second term of the presidency of Ferdinand Marcos")
See also: [1969 Philippine presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_Philippine_presidential_election "1969 Philippine presidential election")
Marcos's second term was characterized by social unrest, beginning with the [1969 balance of payments crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_Philippine_balance_of_payments_crisis "1969 Philippine balance of payments crisis"), which was triggered by exuberant infrastructure spending.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Kasaysayan9ch10-82) Opposition groups began to form, with moderate opposition calling for political reform and radicals espousing revolutionary ideology.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Passionate-119)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Daroy1988-120)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-GazetteHistoryProtest-121) A period of unrest and political violence culminated in Marcos's 1972 declaration of martial law, ending his term early and establishing himself as the constitutional dictator of the Philippines.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-govPhDeclarationMartialLaw-13)
#### 1969 presidential campaign and balance of payments crisis
Main article: [1969 Ferdinand Marcos presidential campaign](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1969_Ferdinand_Marcos_presidential_campaign "1969 Ferdinand Marcos presidential campaign")
#### Assassination plot and social unrest
Main article: [First Quarter Storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Quarter_Storm "First Quarter Storm")
Further information: [Diliman Commune](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diliman_Commune "Diliman Commune")
Early in Marcos's second term, Philippine and United States government officials alleged that a group composed mostly of retired military officers, headed by Liberal Party official [Terry Adevoso](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terry_Adevoso "Terry Adevoso"), had organized a revolutionary junta that sought to discredit and kill Marcos. The plot allegedly included Vice President [Fernando Lopez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_Lopez "Fernando Lopez").[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-122)[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-123)[_[non-primary source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No_original_research#Primary,_secondary_and_tertiary_sources "Wikipedia:No original research")_][[122]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-auto1-124)[_[non-primary source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:No_original_research#Primary,_secondary_and_tertiary_sources "Wikipedia:No original research")_]
In addition to private opposition seeking to supplant Marcos, citizens concerned with the economic crisis and Marcos's spending policies challenged his political program.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-marcosMartialLawNeverAgain-125) In addition to the student revolts, political opposition to the Marcos government grew. Opposition senators [Lorenzo Tañada](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lorenzo_Ta%C3%B1ada "Lorenzo Tañada"), [Jovito Salonga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jovito_Salonga "Jovito Salonga"), and [Jose W. Diokno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_W._Diokno "Jose W. Diokno") accused Marcos of seeking to exceed the two-term constitutional limitation and of increasing authoritarianism.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Kasaysayan9ch10-82)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-marcosMartialLawNeverAgain-125) Organizations opposing Marcos during this period included the NUS, National Students League, and the [Movement of Concerned Citizens for Civil Liberties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Movement_of_Concerned_Citizens_for_Civil_Liberties "Movement of Concerned Citizens for Civil Liberties") (MCCCL), led by Diokno. The MCCCL staged mass rallies, attracting as many as 50 thousand attendees.[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Daroy1988-120)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-GazetteHistoryProtest-121) Media reports classified the various opposition groups as either "moderate" or "radical."[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Daroy1988-120) Moderates included Catholic organizations, civil libertarians, and nationalist politicians who sought political reforms.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Passionate-119) Radicals included labor and student groups who wanted more systemic social and economic reform.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Passionate-119)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-GazetteHistoryProtest-121)
By 1970, campus study sessions on [Marxism–Leninism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marxism%E2%80%93Leninism "Marxism–Leninism") in the Philippines had become common, and many students joined organizations associated with the [National Democracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Democracy_\(Philippines\) "National Democracy \(Philippines\)") movement, including the [Kabataang Makabayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabataang_Makabayan "Kabataang Makabayan") (led by [Jose Maria Sison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Maria_Sison "Jose Maria Sison")), [Samahang Demokratiko ng Kabataan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samahang_Demokratiko_ng_Kabataan "Samahang Demokratiko ng Kabataan"), and [Malayang Pagkakaisa ng Kabataang Pilipino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malayang_Pagkakaisa_ng_Kabataang_Pilipino "Malayang Pagkakaisa ng Kabataang Pilipino").[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Passionate-119)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-GazetteHistoryProtest-121)[[124]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:8-126)[[125]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-127)[[126]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-128) The Marcos administration often made no distinction between the moderate political opposition and the student revolutionaries.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:1-129) Consistent with the [Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War "Cold War") geopolitical framework, in which the Philippines was a key regional ally of the United States against the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party"), Marcos broadly labeled his opposition as communist or, more specifically, [Maoist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maoism "Maoism"). With the participation of the armed forces, Marcos waged a campaign to eliminate the [Communist Party of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_the_Philippines "Communist Party of the Philippines"). emphasizing it as a threat to Philippine society.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-marcosMartialLawNeverAgain-125)[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-RebellionRepressionPh-130): 43 [[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-WorldBank-131)[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-132) According to American foreign policy scholar Richard J. Kessler, Marcos "mythologized the group, investing it with a revolutionary aura that only attracted more supporters."[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:10-96)
Marcos responded to the civil unrest in his January 26, 1970, State of the Nation address. During the address, the [National Union of Students](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Union_of_Students_of_the_Philippines "National Union of Students of the Philippines") (NUS) organized a protest outside Congress, inviting other students to join. As Marcos and his wife Imelda left the building, the students threw stones, a stuffed alligator, and a coffin at them.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-InquirerRememberingFQS-133) Opposition groups quickly grew on campuses. Students declared a week-long boycott of classes and instead met to organize rallies.[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Passionate-119)[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Daroy1988-120) Protests led by student groups continued through the end of the university semester in March, and Marcos deployed military force to quell the demonstrators. This period became known as the [First Quarter Storm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Quarter_Storm "First Quarter Storm").[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-GazetteHistoryProtest-121)[[132]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Aureus_1985-134)[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-RebellionRepressionPh-130) Another major protest took place on January 30, in front of the presidential palace. Activists rammed through the palace gate with a fire truck and charged the grounds, tossing rocks, pillboxes, and [Molotov cocktails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Molotov_cocktails "Molotov cocktails"). At least two activists were killed, and several were injured by police.[[133]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Newsbreak-135) Further major protests included a rally on February 12; a rally on February 18, which set fire to the lobby of the United States embassy; a demonstration on February 26; and marches on March 3 and 17. Some media accounts collectively called these the "seven deadly protests of the First Quarter Storm".[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-7DeadlyProtests-136)[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Lacaba_1982_11%E2%80%9345,_157%E2%80%93178-137)
In total, the protests included 50 to 100 thousand participants. The violent response to the protest further radicalized some moderate students against the Marcos government.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Lacaba_1982_11%E2%80%9345,_157%E2%80%93178-137)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-GazetteHistoryProtest-121)[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Rodis-138)[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Claudio2010-139) A significant number of activists did join the Communist Party of the Philippines and began to relocate from the cities to be more extensively deployed in rural areas, where some became guerillas.[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-140)[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-141) On December 29, 1970, [Philippine Military Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Military_Academy "Philippine Military Academy") instructor [Victor Corpus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victor_Corpus "Victor Corpus") defected from the armed forces to join the armed wing of the Communist Party, the [New People's Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_People's_Army "New People's Army") (NPA), in a raid on the academy armory, capturing rifles, machine guns, grenade launchers, a bazooka, and thousands of rounds of ammunition.[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-142) In 1972, Mao Zedong supplied 1,200 [M14](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M14_rifle "M14 rifle") and [AK-47](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-47 "AK-47") rifles to the NPA aboard the [MV _Karagatan_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MV_Karagatan_incident "MV Karagatan incident") to aid its campaign to defeat the government, part of the [people's war](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_war#List_of_People's_Wars "People's war") doctrine.[[141]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-143)[[142]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-144)[[143]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-145)
#### 1971 constitutional convention
Main article: [Philippine Constitutional Convention of 1971](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Constitutional_Convention_of_1971 "Philippine Constitutional Convention of 1971")
Statesmen and politicians opposed to the Marcos administration mostly focused on political and legal reform, including reform of elections and a call for Marcos to comply with the constitutional two-term limit.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Kasaysayan9ch10-82)[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-GazetteHistoryProtest-121) During his first term, on March 16, 1967, opposition politicians in the Philippine Congress had passed Resolution No. 2, calling for a constitutional convention to address these reforms. Marcos surprised his critics by endorsing the move; historians later noted that Marcos hoped the convention would eliminate the two-term limit on the presidency.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Kasaysayan9ch10-82)[[144]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-DeanAndyBautista20141011-146)[[145]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-ImbongvFerrer-147) On November 10, 1970, a special election was held to elect 320 convention delegates. Prominent delegates included former senators [Raul Manglapus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raul_Manglapus "Raul Manglapus") and [Roseller T. Lim](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roseller_T._Lim "Roseller T. Lim"). Other notable figures who would have careers in politics included [Hilario Davide Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilario_Davide_Jr. "Hilario Davide Jr."), [Marcelo Fernan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcelo_Fernan "Marcelo Fernan"), [Sotero Laurel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sotero_Laurel "Sotero Laurel"), [Nene Pimentel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nene_Pimentel "Nene Pimentel"), [Teofisto Guingona Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teofisto_Guingona_Jr. "Teofisto Guingona Jr."), [Raul Roco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Raul_Roco "Raul Roco"), [Edgardo Angara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgardo_Angara "Edgardo Angara"), [Dick Gordon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dick_Gordon_\(politician\) "Dick Gordon \(politician\)"), and [Margarito Teves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Margarito_Teves "Margarito Teves").[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Kasaysayan9ch10-82): 130 [[146]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-delegates-148)
The convention met on June 1, 1971, at [Quezon City Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quezon_City_Hall "Quezon City Hall").[[147]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-KatePedroso&MinervaGeneralao20160921-149) However, its proceedings were marred by politics and delay. The convention also suffered a serious blow to its credibility in May 1972, when a delegate exposed a bribery scheme implicating First Lady Imelda Marcos, in which delegates were paid to vote for Marcos's position.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Kasaysayan9ch10-82): 133 [[148]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-BantayogQuintero-150) The convention and the investigation into the bribery scheme were eventually shelved when Marcos declared martial law in September 1972 and had eleven opposition delegates arrested.[[149]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-PCIJ20060501-151)
#### Plaza Miranda bombing and false flag allegations
Main articles: [Plaza Miranda bombing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaza_Miranda_bombing "Plaza Miranda bombing") and [1972 Manila bombings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Manila_bombings "1972 Manila bombings")
On August 21, 1971, [a fatal bombing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaza_Miranda_bombing "Plaza Miranda bombing") occurred at [Plaza Miranda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plaza_Miranda "Plaza Miranda") in [Quiapo, Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quiapo,_Manila "Quiapo, Manila"), where the Liberal Party was holding a political campaign rally. The government blamed the bombing on the Communist Party, and Marcos issued Proclamation No. 889, assuming emergency powers and suspending the writ of _[habeas corpus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habeas_corpus "Habeas corpus")_.[[150]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Simafrania2006-152)[[151]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-GovPH-PP889-153) During this period, the government ignored any distinction between moderates and radicals. In response to political persecution, many moderates joined the radicals, massively expanding the underground socialist resistance.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-GazetteHistoryProtest-121)[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Rodis-138)[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Lacaba_1982_11%E2%80%9345,_157%E2%80%93178-137)[[152]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Pimentel2006-154)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_] After the end of military rule, unnamed former Communist officials blamed the Plaza Miranda bombing on [Jose Maria Sison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Maria_Sison "Jose Maria Sison"), whom they said had calculated the bombings to provoke Marcos into further political repression. Sison has denied these claims or any involvement by Aquino or the Communist Party, and the Communist Party has never offered official confirmation.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-washingtonpost.com-155)[[154]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-156)[[155]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-157) Some historians claim Marcos was responsible for the Plaza Miranda bombing, as he is known to have used [false flag](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/False_flag "False flag") operations as a pretext for martial law.[[156]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Donnely&Hassman1987-158)[[157]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-159) United States intelligence documents declassified in the 1990s contained evidence implicating Marcos, provided by a [Central Intelligence Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Agency "Central Intelligence Agency") mole within the armed forces.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Blitz2000-160)
In 1972, a series of bombings in Metro Manila occurred. Marcos again blamed the communists, although the only suspects caught were linked to the [Philippine Constabulary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Constabulary "Philippine Constabulary"). The government also claimed that Ninoy Aquino was involved in the plot.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Brillantes1987-161)[[160]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Overholt-162) The first of these bombings took place on March 15, 1972, and the last took place on September 11, 1972,[[161]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-KatePedroso160921-163) twelve days before martial law was announced on September 23 of that year. Martial law was put to a vote in the [1973 Philippine martial law referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_Philippine_martial_law_referendum "1973 Philippine martial law referendum"), which was marred with controversy[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-philippinesReadr-16): 191 [[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Celoza1997-102) resulting in 90.77% support. Marcos
Another alleged false flag attack occurred in 1972, when the government [staged an attempted assassination](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_ambush_of_Juan_Ponce_Enrile "1972 ambush of Juan Ponce Enrile") of defense minister [Juan Ponce Enrile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Juan_Ponce_Enrile "Juan Ponce Enrile").
### Military dictatorship (1972–1981)
Main article: [Martial law under Ferdinand Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martial_law_under_Ferdinand_Marcos "Martial law under Ferdinand Marcos")
See also: [Proclamation No. 1081](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_No._1081 "Proclamation No. 1081")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f5/Marcos_Declares_Martial_Law.jpg/250px-Marcos_Declares_Martial_Law.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Marcos_Declares_Martial_Law.jpg)September 24, 1972, issue of the Sunday edition of the _Philippine Daily Express_
On the evening of September 23, 1972, shortly after the attempted assassination of Enrile, Marcos [declared martial law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_No._1081 "Proclamation No. 1081") in the Philippines and extended his rule beyond the two-term constitutional limit.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-govPhDeclarationMartialLaw-13)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-fmDeclaresSundayExpress-14)[[162]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-nightDeclared-164)[[163]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-165) Although martial law was formally lifted on January 17, 1981, this marked the beginning of a 14-year period of [autocracy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autocracy "Autocracy") lasting until Marcos fled into exile on February 25, 1986. After 1981, Marcos retained virtually all of his constitutional authority until he was ousted.[[164]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-KaiFrancisco20160922-166) As president of the United States, [Richard Nixon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon "Richard Nixon") approved Marcos's subsequent martial law initiative.[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Blitz2000-160)
Marcos [ruled by decree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rule_by_decree "Rule by decree") during this period, inhibiting [freedom of the press](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freedom_of_the_press "Freedom of the press") and other [civil liberties](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_liberties "Civil liberties"), abrogating Congress, and arresting opposition leaders and militant activists, including [Ninoy Aquino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninoy_Aquino "Ninoy Aquino"), [Jovito Salonga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jovito_Salonga "Jovito Salonga"), and [Jose W. Diokno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_W._Diokno "Jose W. Diokno").[[165]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-167)[[166]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-uslc-28-168) Most were detained without charges, although Aquino was formally charged with murder, illegal possession of firearms, and subversion alongside leaders of the New People's Army.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-asianjournalusa.com-169) Eventually, Marcos claimed that martial law was the prelude to creating a _bagong lipunan_ or "new society" based on new social and political values.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
The early years of martial law met public approval,[[168]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-170)[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Case2013-171): 217  as it was believed to have caused crime rates to drop.[[170]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-172)
#### Bagong Lipunan
"Bagong Lipunan" redirects here. For the song, see [Bagong Pagsilang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bagong_Pagsilang "Bagong Pagsilang").
One of Marcos's rationalizations for martial law stated that there was a need to "reform society" by placing it under the control of a "benevolent dictator" who could guide the undisciplined populace through a period of chaos.[[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Brillantes1987-161): 29 [[159]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Brillantes1987-161): 66 [[171]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-BeltranChingkawShadowsofTyrrany-173) He referred to this social engineering exercise as the _bagong lipunan_ , or "new society".[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-OnyebadiMusicAsAPlatform-174): 13  His administration produced propaganda materials, including speeches, books, lectures, slogans, and numerous songs to promote it.[[172]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-OnyebadiMusicAsAPlatform-174): 13 [[173]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-EsquireBagongSilangSong-175)[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-NaveraMetaphorizingMartialLaw-176) According to Marcos's own book, titled _Notes on the New Society_ , his movement urged the poor and the privileged to work as one for the common goals of society and to achieve the liberation of the Filipino people through [self-realization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-realization "Self-realization").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
Bagong Lipunan marked the first major restructuring of Philippine education since the [Treaty of Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treaty_of_Paris_\(1898\) "Treaty of Paris \(1898\)").[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Maca2018EducationLaborExport-177) It reoriented the teaching of civics and history to entrench constitutional authoritarianism.[[174]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-NaveraMetaphorizingMartialLaw-176)[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Maca2018EducationLaborExport-177)[[176]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-178)[[177]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-PalgraveNewHistoryofSEA-179): 414  In addition, it attempted to synchronize the curriculum with the administration's economic strategy of labor exportation.[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Maca2018EducationLaborExport-177) In order to support the new regime, Marcos also established a youth organization, [Kabataang Barangay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sangguniang_Kabataan "Sangguniang Kabataan"), which was led by Marcos's eldest daughter [Imee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imee_Marcos "Imee Marcos"). Presidential Decree 684, enacted in April 1975, encouraged youths aged 15 to 18 to go to camps and do volunteer work.[[178]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-180)[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-wurf-181): [130](https://books.google.com/books?id=R-oK4ZetPIAC&pg=PA130) The Bagong Lipunan was also intensely anti-Chinese. To instill patriotism among Filipino citizens and prevent the growing number of Chinese schools from propagating foreign ideologies, Marcos issued Presidential Decree No. 176, preventing educational institutions from being established exclusively for foreigners or from offering curriculum exclusively for foreigners and restricting [Chinese language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_language "Chinese language") instruction to not more than 100 minutes per day.[[180]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Suryadinata-2017-182)[[181]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Lee-2013-183)[[182]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-184)
In October 1974, Marcos and PKP-1930 entered into a "national unity agreement", through which PKP-1930 would support certain Bagong Lipunan programs such as land reform, trade union reform, and revitalized relations with the [Soviet bloc](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Bloc "Eastern Bloc").[[179]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-wurf-181): 230 [[183]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-qu-185)
#### Metro Manila Commission
In 1975, Marcos issued Presidential Decree No. 824, placing [Manila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila "Manila"), [Quezon City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quezon_City "Quezon City"), two other cities, twelve municipalities of [Rizal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rizal_\(province\) "Rizal \(province\)"), and [Valenzuela](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valenzuela,_Metro_Manila "Valenzuela, Metro Manila") in [Bulacan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulacan "Bulacan") under the administration of the [Metro Manila Commission](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Manila_Development_Authority "Metropolitan Manila Development Authority") (MMC).[[184]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-PD824-186) He appointed his wife, Imelda, as the head of the MMC in 1976; she would serve until her election to the [Batasang Pambansa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batasang_Pambansa_\(legislature\) "Batasang Pambansa \(legislature\)") in 1978.[[185]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-notmmc-187)[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-ButterfieldGov-188) The office was the second most powerful in the Philippine Republic, with its jurisdiction covering around 20 percent of the population and 70 percent of the economic output of the Philippines, and its budget was second only to that of the national government.[[127]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:1-129)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_] [Carlos P. Romulo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_P._Romulo "Carlos P. Romulo") described Imelda as the "de facto vice president" during this period.[[186]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-ButterfieldGov-188)
#### Militarism
Marcos established a group of key advisors and administrators within the military establishment, known as the Rolex 12. His closest advisors and chief administrators: Enrile, [Fidel Ramos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_Ramos "Fidel Ramos"), and [Fabian Ver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabian_Ver "Fabian Ver") were the chief administrators of martial law. Other members included [Danding Cojuangco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danding_Cojuangco "Danding Cojuangco") and [Lucio Tan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucio_Tan "Lucio Tan").
Between 1972 and 1976, Marcos increased the size of the Philippine military from 65,000 to 270,000 personnel in response to [the fall of South Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Saigon "Fall of Saigon") and other communist victories in the region. Military officers were placed on the [corporate boards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Board_of_directors "Board of directors") of the media, public utilities, development projects, and other private corporations. Marcos also supported the growth of a domestic weapons manufacturing industry and increased military spending.[[187]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-189) Marcos organized the [Civilian Home Defense Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Integrated_Civilian_Home_Defense_Forces "Integrated Civilian Home Defense Forces") to battle communist and Islamic insurgencies. Along with other elements of the Marcos regime, it was accused of inflicting human rights violations on leftists, the NPA, Muslim insurgents, and rebels.[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-auto-190)
Under martial law, the [Communist Party of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communist_Party_of_the_Philippines "Communist Party of the Philippines"), the NPA, and the [National Democratic Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Democratic_Front_of_the_Philippines "National Democratic Front of the Philippines") (NDF) grew significantly.[[128]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-RebellionRepressionPh-130): 43 [[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-marcosMartialLawNeverAgain-125) Despite Marcos's claims in 1981 that the conflict was "substantially contained", the NPA had established a foothold in urban areas, while the NDF formed relationships with legal opposition organizations.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Celoza1997-102): [73](https://books.google.com/books?id=Sp3U1oCNKlgC&pg=PA73) [[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-GovPH-PP2045-191) In the early 1980s, key communist leaders in [Davao City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davao_City "Davao City") were killed, leading the administration to claim the Party's "backbone" in the South had broken.[[190]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-192) However, remaining leaders began a campaign of urban insurrection, which led the international press to label Davao as the "Killing Fields" and the "Murder Capital" of the Philippines.[[191]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-ChapmanPost-193) The violence reached its peak in 1985, with 1,282 military and police deaths and 1,362 civilian deaths.[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-web.stanford.edu-194)
#### Foreign policy
See also: [China–Philippines relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93Philippines_relations "China–Philippines relations") and [Philippines–Taiwan relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines%E2%80%93Taiwan_relations "Philippines–Taiwan relations")
By 1977, the armed forces had quadrupled in size, and over 60,000 Filipinos had been arrested for political reasons. He retained the active support of the United States throughout the period of martial law. From 1972 until 1983, the United States government provided $2.5 billion in bilateral military and economic aid to the Marcos regime, and about $5.5 billion was provided by multilateral institutions such as the [World Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Bank "World Bank").[[193]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-195)
In June 1975, Marcos visited Beijing and signed a joint communication normalizing relations with the People's Republic of China. Among other things, Marcos endorsed the [one China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/One_China "One China") policy.
