In turn, Chinese premier [Zhou Enlai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhou_Enlai "Zhou Enlai") pledged that China would not intervene in the internal affairs of the Philippines nor seek to impose its policies in Asia, a move that isolated the local communist movement that China had financially and militarily supported.[[194]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-196)[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-web.stanford.edu-194) The government subsequently captured New People's Army leaders [Bernabe Buscayno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernabe_Buscayno "Bernabe Buscayno") in 1976 and [Jose Maria Sison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_Maria_Sison "Jose Maria Sison") in 1977.[[153]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-washingtonpost.com-155)[[192]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-web.stanford.edu-194)
During the [presidency of Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Jimmy_Carter "Presidency of Jimmy Carter") in the United States, [Philippines–United States relations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines%E2%80%93United_States_relations "Philippines–United States relations") soured somewhat when Carter targeted the Philippines in his [human rights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights "Human rights") campaign. Despite this, the Carter administration maintained the policy of [military aid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_military_aid "United States military aid") to the Marcos regime to retain U.S. military bases and guard American oil supply lines from the Middle East.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:10-96) Carter successfully pressured Marcos to release Ninoy Aquino.[[195]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-197)[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-JenFrancoElectionsandDemocratization-198): 168  A 1979 [US Senate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Senate "United States Senate") report stated that U.S. officials were aware as early as 1973 that Philippine government agents were in the United States to harass Filipino dissidents. In June 1981, two anti-Marcos labor activists were assassinated outside a union hall in Seattle. On at least one occasion, CIA agents blocked [FBI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation "Federal Bureau of Investigation") investigations of Philippine agents.[[197]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-199)
#### 1978 parliamentary election and prime ministry
In response to international pressure, including from the Carter administration, Marcos announced that the [1978 Philippine parliamentary election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1978_Philippine_parliamentary_election "1978 Philippine parliamentary election") would be held on April 7 to elect 166 regional representatives (out of 208) to an [interim Batasang Pambansa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interim_Batasang_Pambansa "Interim Batasang Pambansa").[[196]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-JenFrancoElectionsandDemocratization-198): 168  Marcos established a new party, the [Kilusang Bagong Lipunan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilusang_Bagong_Lipunan "Kilusang Bagong Lipunan") (KBL), to support his social reform policies. Aquino and his supporters formed [Lakas ng Bayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lakas_ng_Bayan "Lakas ng Bayan") (LABAN), fielding 21 candidates in the Metro Manila region, including Aquino, [Neptali Gonzales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neptali_Gonzales "Neptali Gonzales"), [Teofisto Guingona Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teofisto_Guingona_Jr. "Teofisto Guingona Jr."), [Ramon Mitra Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ramon_Mitra_Jr. "Ramon Mitra Jr."), [Nene Pimentel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nene_Pimentel "Nene Pimentel"), journalist [Napoleon Rama](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon_Rama "Napoleon Rama"), publisher [Alejandro Roces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alejandro_Roces "Alejandro Roces"), and poet-playwright [Soc Rodrigo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soc_Rodrigo "Soc Rodrigo").[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Roces-200) However, LABAN's campaign was restricted, and Marcos refused to allow Aquino out of prison to campaign.[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Case2013-171)
Official results showed the KBL winning 137, while [Pusyon Bisaya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pusyon_Bisaya "Pusyon Bisaya") won 13 seats. LABAN received zero seats. The election was marred by allegations of "pre-stuffed ballot boxes, phony registration, 'flying voters', manipulated election returns, and vote buying."[[169]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Case2013-171): 306  As a result, Marcos became [Prime Minister of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_the_Philippines "Prime Minister of the Philippines"), the first to hold the position since the American occupation. Under Article 9 of the 1973 constitution, Marcos was granted broad executive powers as the official head of government, head of the National Economic Development Authority, and commander-in-chief of the armed forces. All of the powers of the president from the 1935 Constitution were transferred to the prime minister.
Among the candidates elected to the Batasang Pambansa in 1978 was [Imelda Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imelda_Marcos "Imelda Marcos"), who took a leave of absence as governor of the MMC from February 17 to June 12. During that time, Ferdinand served as acting MMC governor.[[199]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-201)
#### Energy and heavy industry policy
In 1979, Marcos added eleven heavy industrialization projects to his economic agenda, prioritizing the production of aluminum, copper, steel, cement, coconut, [phosphatic fertilizer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fertilizer "Fertilizer"), and paper,[[200]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-csmonotor19800919elevenindustrial-202)[[201]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-203) as well as energy projects, including the development of petrochemicals, diesel engines, alcogas, and hydroelectric, geothermal, and nuclear power.[[202]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-204)[[203]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-205)[[204]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-206) The Marcos regime ultimately built seventeen hydroelectric and geothermal plants, with the Philippines becoming the world's second largest geothermal producer in 1983.[[205]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-207)
Although six nuclear power plants were planned, only the [Bataan Nuclear Power Plant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bataan_Nuclear_Power_Plant "Bataan Nuclear Power Plant") (BNPP) was completed. Its construction was paused in 1979 following the [Three Mile Island accident](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Three_Mile_Island_accident "Three Mile Island accident"), and the BNPP was closed shortly after its 1985 completion following the [Chernobyl disaster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chernobyl_disaster "Chernobyl disaster"). Safety reviews have revealed over 4,000 defects, and the site lies near [Mount Pinatubo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Pinatubo "Mount Pinatubo") and three geological faults.[[206]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:5-208)[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:4-88) The construction loans used to build BNPP were only paid off in April 2017, and maintenance costs have exceeded ₱40 million per year.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:4-88)[[207]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-209)
#### Agricultural and food policy
The [World Bank](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Bank_Group "World Bank Group") reported that crops (rice, corn, coconut and sugar), livestock and poultry and fisheries in the Philippines grew at an average rate of 6.8%, 3% and 4.5%, respectively from 1970 to 1980, and while the forestry sector declined by an annual average rate of 4.4% through the 1970s.[[208]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-210) Marcos's signature agricultural program, [Masagana 99](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masagana_99 "Masagana 99"), was launched on May 21, 1973,[[209]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Bettina-211)[[210]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-GovPH-PD27-212) to address a rice shortage.[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-MiguelPaoloJoelandLarah-213) Its goal was to raise yield from 40 to 99 cavans (4.4 tons) per hectare.[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:15-214) The program pushed farmers to use high-yield seeds, fertilizer, and herbicides.[[211]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-MiguelPaoloJoelandLarah-213) Initial success came from encouraging farmers to plant [IR8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IR8 "IR8"), a "miracle rice" funded by the [Rockefeller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rockefeller_Foundation "Rockefeller Foundation") and [Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ford_Foundation "Ford Foundation") foundations and the UPLB CAFS through the [International Rice Research Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Rice_Research_Institute "International Rice Research Institute"),[[213]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Rowlatt20161201-215)[[214]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Chandler1992-216): 7  which had been under development since 1962.[[215]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-BillGanzel-217) This increased rice production from 3.7 to 7.7 million tons in two decades and made the Philippines a rice exporter for the first time in the 20th century.[[216]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-218)[[217]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-219)[[212]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:15-214) However, the switch to IR8 required more fertilizers and pesticides, primarily profiting multinationals' agricultural concerns rather than the majority of small, peasant farmers, who often remained in poverty.[[218]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-220)
### Third term and ouster (1981–1986)
#### End of martial law and 1981 presidential election
Main article: [1981 Philippine presidential election and referendum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1981_Philippine_presidential_election_and_referendum "1981 Philippine presidential election and referendum")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/47/MarcosinWashington1983.jpg/250px-MarcosinWashington1983.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:MarcosinWashington1983.jpg)Marcos on a visit to the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") in 1982
On January 17, 1981, Marcos issued Proclamation 2045, lifting martial law without restoring habeas corpus for rebellion and subversion-related crimes. The proclamation was timed to precede a state visit from [Pope John Paul II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pope_John_Paul_II "Pope John Paul II") and the presidential [inauguration of Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_inauguration_of_Ronald_Reagan "First inauguration of Ronald Reagan") in the United States to minimize international opposition.[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Celoza1997-102): [73](https://books.google.com/books?id=Sp3U1oCNKlgC&pg=PA73) [[189]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-GovPH-PP2045-191)[[219]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-221) Marcos scheduled presidential elections and a referendum on [barangay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barangay "Barangay") elections for June 16, six months after the proclamation. Marcos stood for re-election, but the major opposition parties, led by LABAN, boycotted the election under the banner of the [United Nationalist Democratic Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nationalist_Democratic_Organization "United Nationalist Democratic Organization") (UNIDO). He easily defeated token opposition.[[220]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Steinberg-222)
Marcos' third inauguration took place on Tuesday, June 30, 1981, at the [Quirino Grandstand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quirino_Grandstand "Quirino Grandstand") in Manila.[[221]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-223) Attendees included Singaporean prime minister [Lee Kuan Yew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Kuan_Yew "Lee Kuan Yew"), future [Chinese president](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/President_of_China "President of China") [Yang Shangkun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yang_Shangkun "Yang Shangkun") and [Thai prime minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_Thailand "Prime Minister of Thailand") [Prem Tinsulanonda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prem_Tinsulanonda "Prem Tinsulanonda"). American vice president [George H. W. Bush](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_H._W._Bush "George H. W. Bush") also attended and praised Marcos for his "adherence to democratic principles and to the democratic processes".[[c]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-BushMarcos-228)[[226]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-229)
#### Economic recession
Further information: [Economic history of the Philippines (1965–1986)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_history_of_the_Philippines_\(1965%E2%80%931986\) "Economic history of the Philippines \(1965–1986\)")
During the martial law period, the Philippine economy continued to expand as it had in the decade prior, fueled by the administration's continued reliance on foreign lending, which allowed it to defy international price shocks as a result of the [1973](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1973_oil_crisis "1973 oil crisis") and [1979](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1979_oil_crisis "1979 oil crisis") energy crises. From 1964 to 1982, the [gross domestic product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gross_domestic_product "Gross domestic product") of the Philippines grew from $5.27 billion to $37.14 billion, with approximately 9 percent growth in each of 1973 and 1976. However, external debt also grew from $360 million in 1962 to $17.2 billion in 1980. This debt-driven growth left the nation vulnerable.[[227]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-230) When the United States raised interested rates from 1980 to 1982 in response to high inflation, the Philippine economy went into decline beginning in 1981, producing the worst recession in history by 1985. The economy contracted by 7.3 percent for two consecutive years in 1984 and 1985.[[228]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-EJGuido&CheDeLosReyes20170921-231)[[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-povertyInequalityGrowthPhilippines-232) Poverty rates reached 49 percent.[[229]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-povertyInequalityGrowthPhilippines-232) American economist [James K. Boyce](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_K._Boyce "James K. Boyce") has referred to the Philippine economy under Marcos as an example of "[immiserizing growth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immiserizing_growth "Immiserizing growth")", paradoxically worsening the economy through growth in which the rich get absolutely richer and the poor become absolutely poorer.[[230]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Marcos'_Green_Revolution-233)[_[better source needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability#Questionable_sources "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_]
In particular, the commercial logging and timber industry, which had accounted for five percent of GDP during the first half of the 1970s. Timber products were a top export.[[231]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-234) However, in the early 1980s, the forestry industry collapsed because most accessible forests had been depleted. Of 12 million hectares of forest land, about 7 million had been harvested at a rate of 300,000 per year for the prior two decades.[[232]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-grafStaggering3-235)[[233]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-BoycePolEcoEnvironment-236) In 1981, the [Food and Agriculture Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Food_and_Agriculture_Organization "Food and Agriculture Organization") classified 2 million hectares of Philippine forests "severely degraded and incapable of regeneration".[[234]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-ShairaDeforestation-237)
Economic troubles undermined efforts at a second educational restructuring in 1981.[[175]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Maca2018EducationLaborExport-177)
#### Manila Film Center collapse
Construction on the [Manila Film Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila_Film_Center "Manila Film Center") began in January 1981 at a cost of $25 million.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:4-88)[[235]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-238) In order to meet the January 1982 deadline ahead of the [Manila International Film Festival](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metro_Manila_Film_Festival "Metro Manila Film Festival"), four thousand workers were employed to work in around-the-clock shifts. The lobby was constructed in 72 hours by 1,000 workers.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:4-88) A scaffolding collapsed on November 17, 1981, killing multiple workers. Rescuers and ambulances were kept away for 9 hours after the incident.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:4-88) The collapse became an infamous example of the rushed construction and the Marcoses' [edifice complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edifice_complex "Edifice complex").
#### Ninoy Aquino assassination
Main article: [Assassination of Ninoy Aquino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Ninoy_Aquino "Assassination of Ninoy Aquino")
On August 21, 1983, opposition leader Ninoy Aquino was assassinated on the tarmac at [Manila International Airport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninoy_Aquino_International_Airport "Ninoy Aquino International Airport") upon his return to the country after three years in exile in the United States, where he had a heart bypass operation after Marcos allowed him to seek medical care.[[167]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-asianjournalusa.com-169) The opposition primarily accused Marcos of ordering the assassination through [Fabian Ver](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabian_Ver "Fabian Ver"), while others blamed the military, [Danding Cojuangco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Danding_Cojuangco "Danding Cojuangco"), or [Imelda Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imelda_Marcos "Imelda Marcos"), who had become more influential since her husband's illness.[[236]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-inquirerOrderedHit-239) Ver and other high-ranking military officers were charged with the murder, but they were acquitted in 1985. Their trials were widely judged to be a [miscarriage of justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miscarriage_of_justice "Miscarriage of justice").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] After Marcos was deposed, a reinvestigation of the assassination led to a conviction of sixteen military personnel for the murder, with the [Sandiganbayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandiganbayan "Sandiganbayan") ruling that one of the escorts assigned to Aquino, Rogelio Moreno, had fired the fatal shot.[[237]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:7-240)[[238]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-241)[[239]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-242)
Although government-sanctioned torture declined following the formal end of martial law, killing and disappearances rose after 1981, according to the [Task Force Detainees of the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Task_Force_Detainees_of_the_Philippines "Task Force Detainees of the Philippines").[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-marcosMartialLawNeverAgain-125)
#### Attempted impeachment
By 1984, Marcos also faced significant public and international scrutiny over the widespread reporting of [his family's vast international financial holdings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overseas_landholdings_of_the_Marcos_family "Overseas landholdings of the Marcos family"), and United States president [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan") started distancing himself from the Marcos regime.[[240]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-243) In August 1985, 56 Assemblymen signed a resolution calling for Marcos to be [impeached](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Impeachment "Impeachment") for allegedly diverting United States aid for personal use,[[158]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Blitz2000-160): [167–168](https://books.google.com/books?id=n2rdOhMdCDEC&pg=PA167) citing a July 1985 _[San Jose Mercury News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Jose_Mercury_News "San Jose Mercury News")_ exposé. The impeachment filing included in the complaint the misuse and misapplication of funds "for the construction of the [Manila Film Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Manila_Film_Center "Manila Film Center"), where X-rated and pornographic films are exhibited, contrary to public morals and Filipino customs and traditions".[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] The effort gained little traction, however, and the committee to which the impeachment resolution was referred did not recommend it. Any momentum for removing Marcos under constitutional processes soon died.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
#### 1986 snap election
Main article: [1986 Philippine presidential election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_Philippine_presidential_election "1986 Philippine presidential election")
In late 1985, in the face of escalating public discontent and under pressure from foreign allies, Marcos called a [snap election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snap_election "Snap election") with more than a year left in his term. He selected [Arturo Tolentino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arturo_Tolentino "Arturo Tolentino") as his running mate. The opposition to Marcos united behind Aquino's widow, Corazon, and her running mate, [Salvador Laurel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvador_Laurel "Salvador Laurel").[[241]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-244)[[242]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-245) The religious group [Iglesia ni Cristo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iglesia_ni_Cristo "Iglesia ni Cristo") (INC) endorsed Marcos.[[243]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-246)[[244]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-247)
The campaign period lasted 45 days, from December 19, 1985, to February 5, 1986.[[245]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-bp883-248)[[246]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-International_Observer_Delegation_report-249) Due to his ill health, Marcos was only able to campaign in selected key cities, while Aquino was able to campaign intensively and extensively, even going to remote places from the north of the Philippines to the south of the Philippines.[[247]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-250) On February 4, Marcos declared February 6 and 7 as nationwide public holidays to "give all registered voters fullest opportunity to exercise their right of suffrage."[[248]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-251)
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b9/Corazon_Aquino_inauguration.jpg/250px-Corazon_Aquino_inauguration.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Corazon_Aquino_inauguration.jpg)[Corazon Aquino](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corazon_Aquino "Corazon Aquino"), widow of the assassinated opposition leader [Benigno Aquino Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninoy_Aquino "Ninoy Aquino"), takes the Oath of Office on February 25, 1986.
The elections were held on February 7, 1986.[[249]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-NSM-252) The official election canvasser, the [Commission on Elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commission_on_Elections "Commission on Elections") (COMELEC), declared Marcos the winner. The final tally of the COMELEC had Marcos winning with 10,807,197 votes against Aquino's 9,291,761 votes. On the other hand, the partial 69% tally of the [National Movement for Free Elections](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Movement_for_Free_Elections "National Movement for Free Elections") (NAMFREL), an accredited poll watcher, had Aquino winning with 7,502,601 votes against Marcos's 6,787,556 votes.
The conduct of the election led to popular belief that the polls were tampered with and the results were [fraudulent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Electoral_fraud "Electoral fraud"),[[250]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Mydans19860210-253)[[251]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-FritzandShannon19860124-254) and international observers eventually declared that the "election of February 7 was not conducted in a free and fair manner,"[[246]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-International_Observer_Delegation_report-249) and that the Batasan "ignored explicit provisions of the Philippine Electoral Code requiring that the tampered or altered election returns be set aside during the final counting process, despite protests by representatives of the opposition party."[[246]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-International_Observer_Delegation_report-249) The observers cited cases of vote-buying, intimidation, snatching of ballot boxes, tampered election returns and the disenfranchisement of thousands of voters.[[246]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-International_Observer_Delegation_report-249)[[250]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Mydans19860210-253)[[251]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-FritzandShannon19860124-254)
On February 9, thirty-five computer programmers [walked out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_COMELEC_walkout "1986 COMELEC walkout") of the COMELEC's electronic [quick count](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quick_count "Quick count") at the [Philippine International Convention Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_International_Convention_Center "Philippine International Convention Center"), some fearing for their safety and seeking [sanctuary](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sanctuary#Legal_sanctuary "Sanctuary") in [Baclaran Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baclaran_Church "Baclaran Church"). The technicians—whose protest was broadcast live on national television—claimed that the Marcos camp had manipulated the election results.[[252]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Footage-255)[[253]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-256)
In the last months of Marcos's administration, the [Soviet Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soviet_Union "Soviet Union") stepped up relations and was the only major country to officially congratulate Marcos on his disputed election victory.[[254]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:14-257)[[255]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-258) Marcos had provided favors to the Soviets such as allowing the banned [Philippine Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partido_Komunista_ng_Pilipinas-1930 "Partido Komunista ng Pilipinas-1930") to visit the Soviet Union for consultations.[[254]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:14-257)[[256]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-259)[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:16-105) A [UPI](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Press_International "United Press International") article from March 1986 reported, "Diplomats in Moscow believe the Soviet government totally misjudged Marcos' power to control events. They speculate that Moscow considered his control of legal bodies and his readiness to be 'ruthless' would thwart any popular opposition."[[254]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:14-257)[_[undue weight?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Neutral_point_of_view#Due_and_undue_weight "Wikipedia:Neutral point of view") – [discuss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Talk:Ferdinand_Marcos#undue "Talk:Ferdinand Marcos")_]
#### 1986 aborted Enrile and RAM coup
Main articles: [Reform the Armed Forces Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_the_Armed_Forces_Movement "Reform the Armed Forces Movement") and [February 1986 Reform the Armed Forces Movement coup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_1986_Reform_the_Armed_Forces_Movement_coup "February 1986 Reform the Armed Forces Movement coup")
In the aftermath of the election and the revelations of irregularities, Juan Ponce Enrile and the [Reform the Armed Forces Movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_the_Armed_Forces_Movement "Reform the Armed Forces Movement") (RAM) – a cabal of officers of the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) disgruntled by the [patronage politics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_patronage#Politics "Political patronage") and [corruption](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_corruption "Political corruption") in the AFP, formed in 1982[[257]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-260) – set into motion [a coup attempt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/February_1986_Reform_the_Armed_Forces_Movement_coup "February 1986 Reform the Armed Forces Movement coup") against [Ferdinand and Imelda Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conjugal_dictatorship "Conjugal dictatorship").[[258]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-gringoPlot-261)[[259]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-262) On February 20, RAM approached Corazon Aquino's team to seek their support for the establishment of a planned Junta, but Aquino rejected the offer, seeing it as an attempted power grab by Enrile.[[260]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Fact_Finding_Commission-263)
On February 22, the Enrile and RAM plot was discovered, and on realizing that they could not effectively evade Marcos by running into the mountains of Northern Luzon, Enrile decided that he and Ram would make a last stand in Camp Aguinaldo.[[260]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Fact_Finding_Commission-263)[[261]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-stuartday1-264) Enrile then sought the support of Philippine Constabulary Chief Fidel Ramos, who held Camp Crame across the street, and Ramos decided to side with Enrile against the Marcoses.[[262]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-DavideCommissionReportIV-265)[[261]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-stuartday1-264)
#### Civil disobedience campaign and People Power Revolution
Main article: [People Power Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_Power_Revolution "People Power Revolution")
Responding to the assertions of cheating, Corazon Aquino disputed the COMELEC results and launched a civil disobedience campaign consisting of a series of rallies and a boycott of Marcos crony companies,[[263]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-266) announcing the launch of the campaign in front of two million people[[264]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-SocMvtMob1999-267) at her "_Tagumpay ng Bayan_ " (People's Victory) rally at [Luneta Park](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rizal_Park "Rizal Park") on February 16, 1986.[[264]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-SocMvtMob1999-267)
Corazon Aquino was in Cebu organizing a second major rally when the RAM coup was discovered. Ninoy Aquino's brother Butz immediately organized support for Ramos and Enrile, as did Manila Archbishop Jaime Sin shortly thereafter.[[265]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Duet-268)[[266]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-RapplerYu-269) On the evening of February 22, they urged people to form a human barricade around Camps Aguinaldo and Crame, and people began to flock to the Efipanio de Los Santos Avenue (EDSA) in between the camps in response. Many of these were Corazon Aquino supprters who were already preparing for the next round of rallies in the civil disobedience campaign.[[265]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Duet-268)[[267]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-peoplepower_eyewitness-270) Corazon Aquino flew to Manila and added her support, eventually addressing the crowds on the afternoon of February 24.[[268]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-271)
At 9 in the morning of February 24, Marcos had gone on television and announced he was lifting the "maximum tolerance" policy against Enrile and Ramos' forces, but showed himself on air refusing Fabian Ver's request to fire upon the camps. At the same time, General Josephus Ramas conveyed orders from the President for the Philippine Marines to fire, despite the fact that civilians would be killed in such an attack.[[269]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-McCoyBrothers-272) Colonel Braulio Balbas of the Fourth Marine brigade refused the order, and did so again twenty minutes later when told that "The President is on the other line waiting for compliance!"[[269]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-McCoyBrothers-272) Balbas' refusal on the Morning of February is considered the point when Marcos lost control of the Philippine Marines.[[269]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-McCoyBrothers-272): 251 
Commodore Tagumpay Jardiniano, who was chief of the Naval Defense Force also changed sides on that morning, as had the 15th Strike Wing of the Philippine Air Force.[[270]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-StuartDayThree-273) Consular officials had begun rejecting Marcos' claims of victory as early as February 22, beginning with the Consuls in London, Honolulu, Los Angeles and by February 25 the list included the Philippine Embassies in Washington DC and Moscow.[[271]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-274)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Times_Books-23)
Both Marcos and Aquino now claimed that they had won the election, and thus on February 25, 1986, rival presidential inaugurations were held.[[272]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-275)
The Reagan administration, which had supported Marcos up to that point,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Times_Books-23) finally withdrew its support for Marcos,[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Times_Books-23) and he was eventually forced to flee.[[267]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-peoplepower_eyewitness-270)
## Human rights abuses
Main article: [Human rights abuses of the Marcos dictatorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_rights_abuses_of_the_Marcos_dictatorship "Human rights abuses of the Marcos dictatorship")
See also: [List of torture methods used by the Marcos dictatorship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_torture_methods_used_by_the_Marcos_dictatorship "List of torture methods used by the Marcos dictatorship") and [Extrajudicial killings and forced disappearances in the Philippines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extrajudicial_killings_and_forced_disappearances_in_the_Philippines "Extrajudicial killings and forced disappearances in the Philippines")
The Marcos regime committed documented human rights abuses against a long list of opponents, particularly after the institution of martial law in 1972. These included student activists,[[273]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-iSawMartialLaw-276) farmers,[[274]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-277) journalists,[[275]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-mediaAndMartialLaw-278)[[276]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-writersJournalists-279) legal political opponents,[[277]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-280)[[278]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-tortyur-281)[[198]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Roces-200) and priests and nuns.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Victims were commonly accused of supporting [communist rebels](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_People's_Army "New People's Army") or other leftists or of joining or sympathizing with insurrectionist groups, including the Communist Party, NPA, or [Moro National Liberation Front](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moro_National_Liberation_Front "Moro National Liberation Front").[[279]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-282)[[280]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-283)[[188]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-auto-190) Many were rounded up without an arrest warrant and indefinitely detained without charge.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-marcosMartialLawNeverAgain-125) According to [Rappler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rappler "Rappler"), others were arrested under [color of law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_\(law\) "Color \(law\)") through Arrest Search and Seizure Orders (ASSO), which permitted the military or police to detain citizens.[[281]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-284)
Victims were often taken to safehouses where they were tortured, often blindfolded.[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-marcosMartialLawNeverAgain-125)[[278]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-tortyur-281)[[282]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-mostUnsafe-285)[[283]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-detentionAndTorture-286)[[284]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-martialLawVictimHealing-287) According to activist and abductee [Edgar Jopson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edgar_Jopson "Edgar Jopson"), "Safehouses usually have their windows always shut tight. They are usually covered with high walls. One would usually detect [safehouses] through the traffic of motorcycles and cars going in and out of the house at irregular hours. Burly men, armed with pistols tucked in their waists or in clutch bags, usually drive these vehicles."[[285]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-atenistaMarcosTortureMachine-288)
In many cases, victims were [summarily executed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summary_execution "Summary execution"), and mutilated remains were dumped along roadsides to instill fear and intimidate opponents.[[285]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-atenistaMarcosTortureMachine-288)[[286]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-toYoungFilipinos-289)[[287]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-onSalvaging-290) In many cases, opponents of the regime suddenly [went missing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enforced_disappearance "Enforced disappearance"), without a trace, and their bodies were never recovered.[[288]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-noGraveNoJustice-291) Prominent persons executed or disappeared by the regime included [Liliosa ### Estimates
It is difficult to develop a precise accounting of the abuses under the Marcos regime due to heavy press censorship at the time.[[299]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-inqWarPeaceValor-302)
Estimates of the scale and scope of the human rights abuses under the Marcos regime vary, but estimates generally include approximately 1,500 to 4,000 documented extrajudicial killings or disappearances through targeted assassination or massacres, in addition to the thousands killed in the [Moro conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moro_conflict "Moro conflict").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-hartfordMcCoy-31)[[123]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-marcosMartialLawNeverAgain-125)[[300]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-karinyoMilitar-303)[[301]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-batasMilitar-304)[[302]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-factChecking3257-305)_[[ 303]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-306)_[[304]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-tfdpPumipiglas-307) Tens of thousands more were imprisoned or tortured for political reasons.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-hartfordMcCoy-31)[[301]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-batasMilitar-304)[[302]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-factChecking3257-305)_[[ 305]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-subversiveLives1-308)_ In addition, ten thousand Muslims were killed in the [Moro conflict](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moro_conflict "Moro conflict") by the army, constabulary, and paramilitary groups, many in massacres.[[306]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-pcijMindanaoMemoryMassacres-309)
### Denial by the Marcos family and allies
Main article: [Historical distortion regarding Ferdinand Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Historical_distortion_regarding_Ferdinand_Marcos "Historical distortion regarding Ferdinand Marcos")
Members of the Marcos family deny any responsibility for human rights violations.[[307]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-martialLawHorrorsFabricated-310) [Bongbong Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bongbong_Marcos "Bongbong Marcos") has described claims of human rights abuses as "self-serving statements by politicians, self-aggrandizement narratives, pompous declarations, and political posturing and propaganda."[[308]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-mlLateStrongmanSon-311)[[309]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-enrilesMemoir-312)
Imee called the allegations political accusations. According to her, "If what is demanded is an admission of guilt, I don't think that's possible. Why would we admit to something we did not do?"[[310]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-politicalAccusations-313)

## Exile (1986–1989)
### Flight to Hawaii
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b0/President_Ronald_Reagan_with_President_of_The_Philippines_Ferdinand_Marcos_and_Imelda_Marcos_During_a_State_Visit_Outside_The_Oval_Office_-_DPLA_-_007d99243973a7b4c3b32a011f991aa1.jpg/250px-thumbnail.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:President_Ronald_Reagan_with_President_of_The_Philippines_Ferdinand_Marcos_and_Imelda_Marcos_During_a_State_Visit_Outside_The_Oval_Office_-_DPLA_-_007d99243973a7b4c3b32a011f991aa1.jpg)Ferdinand and Imelda Marcos at the White House with US president [Ronald Reagan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan "Ronald Reagan") in 1982
At 15:00 [PST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Standard_Time "Philippine Standard Time") ([GMT+8](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GMT+8 "GMT+8")) on February 25, 1986, Marcos talked to United States Senator [Paul Laxalt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Laxalt "Paul Laxalt"), a close associate of President Reagan, asking for advice. Laxalt advised him to "cut and cut cleanly", to which Marcos expressed his disappointment.[[321]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-324) In the afternoon, Marcos talked to Enrile, asking for safe passage for him and his family, including close allies such as General Ver. Finally, at 9:00 p.m., the Marcos family was transported by four [Sikorsky HH-3E](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sikorsky_S-61R "Sikorsky S-61R") [helicopters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Helicopter "Helicopter")[[322]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Halperin-325) to [Clark Air Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Air_Base "Clark Air Base") in [Angeles City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angeles_City "Angeles City"), about 83 kilometers north of Manila, before boarding [US Air Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Air_Force "United States Air Force") [C-130](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/C-130 "C-130") planes bound for [Andersen Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andersen_Air_Force_Base "Andersen Air Force Base") in [Guam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guam "Guam") and finally to [Hickam Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hickam_Air_Force_Base "Hickam Air Force Base") in [Hawaii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii "Hawaii"), where Marcos arrived on February 26.[[323]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-326) He also brought with him 22 crates of cash valued at $717 million, 300 crates of assorted [jewelry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jewelry "Jewelry"), $4 million worth of unset precious gems, 65 Seiko and Cartier watches, a 12 by 4 ft box full of [pearls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pearl "Pearl"), a 3 ft solid [gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold "Gold") statue covered in [diamonds](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diamond "Diamond") and other precious stones, $200,000 in gold bullion, nearly $1 million in Philippine pesos, and deposit slips to banks in the United States, Switzerland, and the Cayman Islands worth $124 million.[[324]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-327) His mother, Josefa, was left in [Malacañang Palace](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malaca%C3%B1ang_Palace "Malacañang Palace"). She died in 1988.[[325]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-NYT19860330-328)
Initially, there was confusion in Washington as to what to do with Marcos and the 90 members of his entourage.[[326]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-AP-329) Given the special relations Marcos nurtured with Reagan, the former had expectations of favorable treatment. However, Reagan kept his distance. The [State Department](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/State_Department "State Department") in turn assigned former deputy chief of mission to Manila, [Robert G. Rich Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_G._Rich_Jr. "Robert G. Rich Jr."), to be the point of contact. The entourage was first billeted inside the housing facilities of [Hickam Air Force Base](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hickam_Air_Force_Base "Hickam Air Force Base"). The State Department announced the Marcoses were not immune from legal charges, and within weeks hundreds of cases had been filed against them.[[327]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-ADST_-_Handholding_a_Dictator-330)
Throughout his stay in Hawaii, he and his family enjoyed a high life, living in a luxurious house in [Makiki Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makiki_Heights "Makiki Heights"), as Imelda entertained guests at parties,[[328]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-331) while Filipinos back in the Philippines suffered under the debt Marcos incurred.[[329]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-332)
When protestors stormed Malacañang Palace shortly after their departure, it was notoriously discovered that Imelda had left behind over 2,700 pairs of shoes.[[330]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-333) The protesters looted and vandalized the palace; many stole documents, jewelry, food, typewriters, etc.[[331]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-334)
The Catholic hierarchy and Manila's [middle class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_class "Middle class") were crucial to the success of the revolution. Contrary to the widely held notion that the protests were limited to Manila, protests against Marcos also occurred in the provinces and on the islands of Visayas and Mindanao.[[332]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-335)[[333]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-336)
### Plans to return and "The Marcos Tapes"
More than a year after the revolution, it was revealed to the [United States House Foreign Affairs subcommittee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_House_Foreign_Affairs_Subcommittee_on_Asia_and_the_Pacific "United States House Foreign Affairs Subcommittee on Asia and the Pacific") in 1987 that Marcos held an intention to return to the Philippines and overthrow the Aquino government. American attorney Richard Hirschfeld and business consultant Robert Chastain, both of whom posed as arms dealers, gained knowledge of a plot by gaining Marcos's trust and secretly recorded their conversations with the ousted leader.
According to Hirschfeld, he was first invited by Marcos to a party held at the latter's family residence in Honolulu. After hearing that one of Hirschfeld's clients was Saudi Sheikh Mohammad Fassi, Marcos's interest was piqued because he had done business with Saudis in the past. A few weeks later, Marcos asked for help with securing a passport from another country in order to travel to the Philippines while bypassing travel restrictions imposed by the Philippines and United States governments. This failed, however, and subsequently Marcos asked Hirschfeld to arrange a $10-million loan from Fassi.
On January 12, 1987, Marcos stated to Hirschfeld that he required another $5 million loan "in order to pay 10,000 soldiers $500 each as a form of 'combat life insurance.'" When asked by Hirschfeld if he was talking about an invasion of the Philippines, Marcos responded, "Yes". Hirschfeld stated that Marcos said that he was negotiating with several arms dealers to purchase up to $18 million worth of weapons, including tanks and heat-seeking missiles, and enough ammunition to "last an army three months".
Marcos had thought of flying to his hometown in Ilocos Norte and initiating a plot to kidnap Corazon Aquino. "What I would like to see happen is we take her hostage," Marcos told Chastain. "Not to hurt her ... no reason to hurt her ... to take her."
Learning of this plan, Hirschfeld contacted the [US Department of Justice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Justice "United States Department of Justice") and was asked for further evidence. This information eventually reached President Ronald Reagan, who placed Marcos under "island arrest", further limiting his movement.[[334]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-337)[[335]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-338)
### Legal cases
Within two weeks of his arrival to the United States, hundreds of criminal and civil cases against the Marcos clique were filed in Hawaii, San Francisco, and New York.[[327]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-ADST_-_Handholding_a_Dictator-330) Marcos made personal appeals to Reagan to put a stop to these cases. In June 1988 [National Security Advisor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Security_Advisor "United States National Security Advisor") [Colin Powell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Powell "Colin Powell") recommended proceeding with indictments of the Marcoses as he reviewed the cases as forwarded by [United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Attorney_for_the_Southern_District_of_New_York "United States Attorney for the Southern District of New York") [Rudy Giuliani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rudy_Giuliani "Rudy Giuliani"). Reagan tacitly approved.[[336]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-RRPL_-_Box_153-339) On August 4, Marcos stated that he had [head of state immunity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Immunity_from_prosecution_\(international_law\) "Immunity from prosecution \(international law\)") to resist subpoenas by a [federal grand jury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_juries_in_the_United_States#Federal_law "Grand juries in the United States") to produce his finger and palm prints and failed to consent to investigators to review his bank accounts. By August 18, a bench warrant of arrest was issued against the Marcoses. By October of that year, Reagan personally wrote to Marcos, informing him that he believed in his innocence of the charges against him but reminding him that the case was out of his hands. He assured him that they would have every opportunity to prove their innocence.[[337]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-RRPL_-_CO125-340)
Giuliani pressed for indicting the Marcoses for violating the [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racketeer_Influenced_and_Corrupt_Organizations_Act "Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act") (RICO). The RICO Act focuses specifically on [racketeering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racketeering "Racketeering") and allows the leaders of a syndicate to be tried for the crimes they [ordered](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirty_hands "Dirty hands") others to do [or assisted them in doing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enmund_v._Florida "Enmund v. Florida"). For example, before RICO, a person who instructed someone else to [murder](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder "Murder") could be exempt from prosecution because they did not personally commit the crime. In his next letter to President Reagan on October 20, Marcos complained that Giuliani was giving them nothing but an ultimatum to plead guilty and even to testify against others, including his own family.[[337]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-RRPL_-_CO125-340)
## Personal life
### Marriages and children
Marcos lived with a [common-law wife](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Common-law_marriage "Common-law marriage"), Carmen Ortega, an [Ilocana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ilocano_people "Ilocano people") [mestiza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Filipino_Mestizos "Filipino Mestizos") who was the 1949 Miss Press Photography. They had three children and resided for about two years at 204 Ortega Street in [San Juan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Juan,_Metro_Manila "San Juan, Metro Manila"). In August 1953, their engagement was announced in Manila dailies.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-loveLiesLoot-4) Not much is known about what happened to Ortega and their children.
Marcos, who was baptized and raised into the [Philippine Independent Church](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Independent_Church "Philippine Independent Church"),[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-Celoza1997-102): 23  subsequently converted to [Catholicism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church") in later life to marry [Imelda Trinidad Romualdez](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imelda_Marcos "Imelda Marcos").[[338]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-341) They married on April 17, 1954, 11 days after they first met. They had three biological children: [Imee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imee_Marcos "Imee Marcos"), [Bongbong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bongbong_Marcos "Bongbong Marcos"), and [Irene Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Irene_Marcos "Irene Marcos").[[339]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-govph-342) Marcos's fourth child with Ortega was born after his marriage to Imelda.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-FOOTNOTEMijares1976-79)[_[page needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citing_sources "Wikipedia:Citing sources")_] Marcos and Imelda later adopted a daughter, [Aimee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aimee_Marcos "Aimee Marcos").[[340]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-343)
### Extramarital affairs
Marcos had an affair with American actress [Dovie Beams](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dovie_Beams "Dovie Beams") from 1968 to 1970. According to reports by the _[Sydney Morning Herald](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sydney_Morning_Herald "Sydney Morning Herald")_ , Marcos also had an affair with former _Playboy_ model Evelin Hegyesi around 1970 and sired a child with her, Analisa Josefa.[[341]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-formerModel-344)[[342]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-345)
## Death and burial
Main article: [Burial of Ferdinand Marcos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Burial_of_Ferdinand_Marcos "Burial of Ferdinand Marcos")
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e0/Ferdinand_E._Marcos_Presidential_Center_sign.jpg/250px-Ferdinand_E._Marcos_Presidential_Center_sign.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ferdinand_E._Marcos_Presidential_Center_sign.jpg)The body of Marcos was stored in a refrigerated crypt at the [Ferdinand E. Marcos Presidential Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_E._Marcos_Presidential_Center "Ferdinand E. Marcos Presidential Center") in Batac, Ilocos Norte until 2016.
Marcos was admitted to the hospital on January 15, 1989, with pneumonia and underwent a series of operations.[[343]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-346) In his dying days, Marcos was visited by Vice President Salvador Laurel.[[344]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-347) During the visit, Marcos offered to return 90% of his ill-gotten wealth to the Filipino people in exchange for a burial in the Philippines besides his mother, an offer also disclosed to [Enrique Zobel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enrique_Zobel "Enrique Zobel"). However, Marcos's offer was rebuffed by the [Aquino government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Corazon_Aquino "Presidency of Corazon Aquino") and by Imelda.[[345]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-348)[[346]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-349)[[347]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-350)
Marcos died at St. Francis Medical Center in [Honolulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Honolulu "Honolulu") at 12:40 a.m. ([HST](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii%E2%80%93Aleutian_Time_Zone "Hawaii–Aleutian Time Zone")) on September 28, 1989, of kidney, heart, and lung ailments, 17 days after his 72nd birthday.[[348]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-351) Moments after, [the younger Ferdinand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bongbong_Marcos "Bongbong Marcos") eulogised his late father by stating, "Hopefully friends and detractors alike will look beyond the man to see what he stood for: his vision, his compassion, and his total love of country."[[349]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-352)
Marcos was interred in a private mausoleum at [Byodo-In Temple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Byodo-In_\(Hawaii\) "Byodo-In \(Hawaii\)") on the island of Oahu.
According to [Roberto Ongpin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roberto_Ongpin "Roberto Ongpin"),[[350]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-robongpn-353) Marcos had two kidney transplants. The first one came from his son Bongbong but was rejected by his body. Several years later, soldier in the [presidential security group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Security_Command "Presidential Security Command") who was from his [Batac](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batac "Batac") hometown in Ilocos Norte was the donor. The organ kept him alive until he died.
The Aquino government initially refused to allow Marcos's body to be brought back to the Philippines, which ultimately happened four years later.[[351]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-354)
From 1993 to 2016, Marcos's remains were interred inside a refrigerated, frozen crypt in Batac, Ilocos Norte, where his son, [Ferdinand Jr.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bongbong_Marcos "Bongbong Marcos"), and eldest daughter, [Imee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imee_Marcos "Imee Marcos"), became the local governor and congressional representative, respectively.
[A large bust](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bust_of_Ferdinand_Marcos "Bust of Ferdinand Marcos") of Ferdinand Marcos (inspired by [Mount Rushmore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mount_Rushmore "Mount Rushmore")) was commissioned by the tourism minister, [Jose Aspiras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jose_D._Aspiras "Jose D. Aspiras"), and carved into a hillside in Benguet. It was subsequently destroyed, allegedly by left-wing activists, members of a local tribe who had been displaced by construction of the monument, and looters hunting for the legendary [Yamashita treasure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yamashita's_gold "Yamashita's gold").[[352]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-355)
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a3/Marcos_burial_Ateneans_protest.jpg/250px-Marcos_burial_Ateneans_protest.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Marcos_burial_Ateneans_protest.jpg)Students of the [Ateneo de Manila University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ateneo_de_Manila_University "Ateneo de Manila University") protesting the burial of Marcos
On November 18, 2016, his remains were reburied at the [Libingan ng mga Bayani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Libingan_ng_mga_Bayani "Libingan ng mga Bayani"), ordered by President [Rodrigo Duterte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodrigo_Duterte "Rodrigo Duterte") despite opposition from various groups. On the morning of November 18, using Philippine Armed Forces helicopters, his family and their supporters flew his remains from Ilocos to Manila for a private burial. This account was challenged, and the physical location of his remains is disputed.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-contested-1) Various groups protested the burial.[[353]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-356)[[354]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-357)
## Posthumous lawsuits
### _Roxas v. Marcos_
[Rogelio Roxas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rogelio_Roxas "Rogelio Roxas"), a Filipino treasure hunter, discovered a 3-foot-tall golden Buddha statue in tunnels under the Baguio General Hospital in 1971. Roxas was later arrested and tortured by members of the military, and the statue was taken away. Upon the exile of the Marcoses, Roxas assigned his rights to a friend in the United States and formed the Golden Buddha Corporation (GBC), which pursued the case against the former president. In 1996, the lower court awarded US$22 billion in favor of GBC, the largest sum in a civil case in the history of the United States. In November 1998, the [Hawaii Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hawaii_Supreme_Court "Hawaii Supreme Court") overturned the ruling but maintained an award of US$6 million for the illegal arrest and torture experienced by Roxas.[[355]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-AP_-_$22B_Award_Reversed-358)[[356]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-uniset.ca-359)
### Sandiganbayan, Supreme Court, and international trials
[![](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/9f/Ferdinand_Marcos_with_Emmanuel_Pelaez.jpg/250px-Ferdinand_Marcos_with_Emmanuel_Pelaez.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ferdinand_Marcos_with_Emmanuel_Pelaez.jpg)Ferdinand Marcos with Emmanuel Pelaez
On November 9, 2018, Imelda Marcos was found "guilty beyond reasonable doubt" by the Sandiganbayan of seven counts of graft for private organizations set up in Switzerland during her time as a government official from 1968 to 1986. In less than 20 days, however, the Sandiganbayan listed Imelda's "advanced age" and health condition as considerations for allowing the accused to post bail. The Fifth Division's (of the Sandiganbayan) ruling read that "the fact that she is of advanced age and for health reasons, consistent with the doctrine in Enrile vs. Sandiganbayan, bail is allowed for these seven cases."[[357]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-360) The Supreme Court of the Philippines affirmed that the family's assets, beyond their government salaries, are considered ill-gotten wealth. In 1998 the Court acquitted Imelda Marcos of corruption charges from a previous graft conviction in 1993.
The US Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals confirmed a contempt judgement in relation to the assets of Imelda and her son [Bongbong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bongbong_Marcos "Bongbong Marcos"). Although on a different matter, this judgement awarded $353.6 million to human rights victims, which was arguably the largest contempt award ever affirmed by an appellate court.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]
### Wealth and reparations
From 1989 to 1996, a series of civil suits were filed against Marcos and his daughter Imee, alleging that they bore responsibility for executions, torture, and disappearances under his regime. A jury award for US$2 billion was overturned on June 12, 2008, by the Supreme Court of the United States in _[Republic of Philippines v. Pimentel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Philippines_v._Pimentel "Republic of Philippines v. Pimentel")_. The Court ruled 7–2 that
In 1995, some 10,000 Filipinos won a US [class-action](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class-action "Class-action") lawsuit filed against the Marcos estate. The claims were filed by victims or their surviving relatives consequent to torture, execution, and disappearances.[[358]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-361)[[359]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-362)
The [Swiss government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Switzerland "Government of Switzerland"), initially reluctant to respond to allegations that stolen funds were held in Swiss accounts,[[360]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-363) returned $684 million of Marcos' holdings.[[361]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-star-364)[[362]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-365)[[363]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-366)
Corazon Aquino repealed many of the repressive laws enacted during Marcos's dictatorship. She restored the right of _habeas corpus_ , repealed anti-labor laws, and freed hundreds of [political prisoners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_prisoners "Political prisoners").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-philippinesReadr-16): 361 
From 1989 to 1996, a series of suits were brought before US courts against Marcos and his daughter Imee, alleging that they bore responsibility for executions, torture, and disappearances. A jury in the [Ninth Circuit Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninth_Circuit_Court_of_Appeals "Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals") awarded US$2 billion to the plaintiffs and to a [class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_action_lawsuit "Class action lawsuit") composed of human rights victims and their families.[[364]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-367) On June 12, 2008, in _[Republic of Philippines v. Pimentel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_Philippines_v._Pimentel "Republic of Philippines v. Pimentel")_ , the [US Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_United_States "Supreme Court of the United States") ruled 7–2 that "The judgment of the Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit is reversed, and the case is remanded with instructions to order the District Court to dismiss the [interpleader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpleader "Interpleader") action." The court dismissed the interpleader lawsuit filed to determine the rights of 9,500 Filipino human rights victims (1972–1986) to recover US$35 million, part of a US$2 billion judgment in US courts against the Marcos estate, because the Philippine government is an indispensable party, protected by [sovereign immunity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sovereign_immunity "Sovereign immunity"). The Philippine government claimed ownership of the funds transferred by Marcos in 1972 to [Arelma S.A.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arelma_S.A. "Arelma S.A."), which invested the money with [Merrill Lynch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Merrill_Lynch "Merrill Lynch"), Pierce, Fenner & Smith Inc. in New York.[[365]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-368)[[366]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-369)[[367]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-370) In July 2017, the Philippine Court of Appeals rejected the petition seeking to enforce the United States court decision.[[368]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-371)
In 2013, Philippine Congress passed Republic Act 10368 or the Human Rights Victims Reparation and Recognition Act of 2013.[[369]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:0-372) The law created the Human Rights Violations Claims Board and provided reparations to victims of summary execution, torture, enforced disappearances, and other human rights violations.[[370]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:9-373) Compensation came from P10 billion of stolen wealth seized by the government from the Marcoses.[[371]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-374) A total of 11,103 victims received compensation in 2018.[[369]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:0-372) A bill filed in Congress in 2020 proposed to compensate tens of thousands of people still not officially recognized as victims of state-sponsored violence.[[370]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-:9-373)
In 2012, the [Philippine Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippine_Supreme_Court "Philippine Supreme Court") ruled all Marcos assets beyond legally declared earnings/salary to be ill-gotten wealth[[372]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-scImeldaMarcosvsRP-375) and such wealth to have been forfeited to the government or human rights victims.[[373]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-376)
According to the [Presidential Commission on Good Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidential_Commission_on_Good_Government "Presidential Commission on Good Government") (PCOG), the Marcos family and their cronies looted so much wealth from the Philippines that investigators have not determined precisely how many billions were stolen.[[374]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-NYTimesHuntForMarcosBillions-377) PCOG estimated that Marcos stole around $5 billion to $10 billion[[375]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-378) while earning an annual salary equivalent to US$13,500.[[376]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-The10BQuestion-379)
Among the sources of the Marcos wealth are alleged to be diverted foreign aid, military aid (including to Marcos for sending Filipino troops to Vietnam), and kickbacks from public works contracts.[[377]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-timeTakingTollMartialLawVictims-380)
In 1990, Imelda Marcos was acquitted of charges that she raided the Philippine treasury by a US jury. She was acquitted because the jury deemed that the US did not have jurisdiction.[[378]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-381)[[379]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-382) In 1993, she was convicted of graft in Manila for entering into three unfavourable lease contracts between a government-run transportation agency and another government-run hospital.[[380]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-383) In 1998, the Philippine Supreme Court overturned her conviction.[[381]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-384) In 2008, Philippine trial court judge Silvino Pampilo acquitted Imelda of 32 counts of illegal money transfer[[382]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-nyTimesImeldaAcquitted-385) from the 1993 graft conviction.[[383]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-imeldaGraft1993-386) In 2010, she was ordered to repay the Philippine government almost $280,000 for funds taken in 1983.[[384]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-imeldaMarcosFastFacts-387) In 2012, a US Court of Appeals of the Ninth Circuit upheld a contempt judgement against Imelda and Bongbong for violating an injunction barring them from dissipating their assets and awarded $353.6 million to human rights victims.[[385]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-marcosLosesUSAppeal-388) As of October 2015, she faced 10 graft charges and 25 civil cases,[[386]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-wsj.com-389)[[387]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-newsinfo.inquirer.net-390) down from 900 in the 1990s, as most cases were dismissed for lack of evidence.[[388]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-gmanetwork.com-391)[_[needs update](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Manual_of_Style/Dates_and_numbers#Chronological_items "Wikipedia:Manual of Style/Dates and numbers")_]
In the 2004 _Global Corruption Report_ , Marcos appeared in the list of the world's most corrupt leaders, behind [Suharto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suharto "Suharto").[[389]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-transparency.org-392) One of Marcos's former ministers of industry, [Vicente Paterno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vicente_Paterno "Vicente Paterno"),[[390]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-paterno1-393) noted that while the amount stolen by Marcos's regime probably fell short of Suharto's, Marcos invested outside the Philippines, whereas Suharto mostly invested at home.[[390]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-paterno1-393)
The [International Consortium of Investigative Journalists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_Consortium_of_Investigative_Journalists "International Consortium of Investigative Journalists")' (ICIJ) exposé of [offshore leaks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Offshore_leaks "Offshore leaks") accused Imee of hiding wealth in [tax havens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tax_haven "Tax haven") in the [British Virgin Islands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Virgin_Islands "British Virgin Islands").[[391]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-ICIJ_Secret_Files_Expose-394)[[392]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-395)
In 2014, Imelda's former secretary Vilma Bautista was sentenced to prison for conspiring to sell a [Monet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monet "Monet"), [Sisley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sisley "Sisley"), and other masterpieces.[[393]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-inqMarcosSecretaryMonet-396)[[394]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-397)
On May 9, 2016, ICIJ released the [Panama Papers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Panama_Papers "Panama Papers").[[395]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-398) Imee and Irene[[396]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-399) were named, along with grandsons Fernando Manotoc, Matthew Joseph Manotoc; and Ferdinand Richard Manotoc, his son-in-law Gregorio Maria Araneta III;[[397]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-400) including his son-in-law Tommy Manotoc's relatives Ricardo Gabriel Manotoc and Teodoro Kalaw Manotoc.[[398]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-401)
On September 3, 2017, then-President [Rodrigo Duterte](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodrigo_Duterte "Rodrigo Duterte") said the Marcos family was ready to transfer their wealth to the government.[[399]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-402) In January 2018, a draft House Bill proposing a settlement and immunity for the Marcoses was received by the Duterte government in July 2017.[[400]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-cnnMarcosDealDuterte-403)[[401]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-fbDuterteMarcosHousebill-404)
## Publications
Marcos published various books during his term from 1970 to 1983, and a final offering was published posthumously in 1990.[[402]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-iLib-405) Apparently these books were written by [ghostwriters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghostwriter "Ghostwriter"), notably [Adrian Cristobal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adrian_Cristobal "Adrian Cristobal").[[403]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-406)[[404]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-407)[[405]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ferdinand_Marcos#cite_note-408)
  * _National Discipline: the Key to Our Future_ (1970)
  * _Today's Revolution: Democracy_ (1971)
  * _Notes on the New Society of the Philippines_ (1973)
  * _Tadhana: the History of the Filipino People_ (1977, 1982)
  * _The Democratic Revolution in the Philippines_ (1977)
  * _Five Years of the New Society_ (1978)
  * _President Ferdinand E. Marcos on law, development and human rights_ (1978)
  * _President Ferdinand E. Marcos on agrarian reform_ (1979)
  * _An Ideology for Filipinos_ (1980)
  * _An Introduction to the Politics of Transition_ (1980)
  * _Marcos's Notes for the[Cancun Summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North%E2%80%93South_Summit "North–South Summit"), 1981_ (1981)
  * _Progress and Martial Law_ (1981)
  * _The New Philippine Republic: A Third World Approach to Democracy_ (1982)
  * _Toward a New Partnership: The Filipino Ideology_ (1983)
  * _A Trilogy on the Transformation of Philippine Society_ (1990)
